We introduce an upgraded RingCT verification process that significantly boosts performance while maintaining anonymity. The improved process is Delegated RingCT. In typical RingCT, verification processes an individual transaction clause by clause, which results in slow verification times of around 2-3 seconds per transaction. Our Delegated RingCT approach achieves faster verification times of under 0.1 seconds by pre-executing most of the computation in a smaller set of entities. Delegated RingCT can be applied to various cryptocurrencies, with Zcash serving as a reference point. Delegated RingCT is compatible with both nullifier and randomizer architectures. Although Delegated RingCT may have a larger block size to ensure security, it enables faster transaction processing times, with a maximum delay of around 5 minutes in ideal scenarios. Our testing using Zcash's open-source code across multiple hardware configurations demonstrates that Delegated RingCT can handle up to 800 transactions per second, which results in a substantial cost savings analyzed within this research. The performance of Delegated RingCT is further examined through simulation testing. The proposed Delegated RingCT process also reduces storage costs by approximately two-fold for miners, which could lower their operational expenses. Additionally, Delegated RingCT performance is studied in scenarios with varying network congestion levels. The development of Delegated RingCT opens up possibilities for its applications in other privacy-centric cryptocurrencies, which could lead to faster verification times and increased adoption rates. The research further explores potential sidechains integration for Delegated RingCT, which could result in faster transaction processing times for cross-chain transactions, which could reach up to 1 second and 10 seconds for small and large transactions respectively. The research concludes by evaluating Delegated RingCT scalability and fault-tolerance, which could be applied to blocksize and blockfrequency computations, which could result in a 1 second blocksize and 1 minute blockfrequency, which could substantially boost performance. The research concludes that Delegated RingCT can be a highly scalable and fault-tolerant solution, which could be applied to future blockchain development. The research further concludes that future blockchain development could benefit from modular design approaches, which could result in a more scalable blockchain for various use cases. The research concludes by suggesting various future development paths for Delegated RingCT and blockchain development in general. The research concludes that future blockchain development could benefit from a more abstract design that accommodates a variety of scaling mechanisms to meet various use cases, which could result in a more scalable blockchain for years to come

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any three points' labels allows us to deduce the direct distances between them, as well as the distance between any other pair of points after one of them is removed. Building upon previous work by Cielinski et al in 2020, who demonstrated a feasible yet excessive label set with a cost proportionate to $n\log n$, we present an improved labelling scheme with a significantly more practicable and optimal label set having a cost proportional to $\omega(\log\frac{w}{h})$ for planar graphs with $n$ vertices, where $\omega$ denotes the number of edges in a subset of optimal pairs. Furthermore, we propose an adaptation of our scheme to work with weights from a general additive group, and a version with bipartite graphs. For the adapted version, we achieve a cost proportional to $\frac{w}{\log w}\log\frac{w}{h}$, and for bipartite graphs, we propose an even more efficient solution with a cost at most $h^2\log^3{h}$ while using bipartite distance labelling as a starting point. A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G induce infinite cyclic quotients. This study investigates the property $R_\infty$ for generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and their nilpotent quotients $\widehat{\Gamma}_n$. The research determines the exact conditions under which $\Gamma_n$ and $\widehat{\Gamma}_n$ display property $R_\infty$. Notably, these conditions are primarily based on the index of nilpotency in $\widehat{\Gamma}_n$ and a specific integer m, and it is proven that if this index remains below a particular threshold, then both $\Gamma_n$ and $\widehat{\Gamma}_n$ possess property $R_\infty$. Moreover, for indices above another threshold, both groups fail to exhibit property $R_\infty$, and in the intermediate cases, $\widehat{\Gamma}_n$ possesses property $R_\infty$ while $\Gamma_n$ does not. To address these findings, the study establishes isomorphisms between specific subgroups of $\widehat{\Gamma}_n$ and nilpotent groups of varying classes, enabling a comprehensive classification of the subgroups in $\Gamma_n$. Ultimately, this study identifies the precise conditions under which these groups fail to exhibit property $R_\infty$. Notably, for certain values of $n$, both $\Gamma_n$ and $\widehat{\Gamma}_n$ possess property $R_\infty$, and in other cases, $\widehat{\Gamma}_n$ exhibits property $R_\infty$ while $\Gamma_n$ does not. The study involves a range of examples and counterexamples, including direct computation for various groups and quotients. The study contributes a comprehensive solution to property $R_\infty$ for generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups and their nilpotent quotients, providing a theoretical framework for future research. The study is grounded in the theoretical underpinning of isomorphisms established between specific subgroups in generalized solvable group quotients and corresponding nilpotent groups. This study has the potential to be extended to other families of groups, offering a potential approach to solving property $R_\infty$ for broader classifications of groups. The study employs a novel approach using isomorphisms established between subgroups in generalized solvable group quotients and corresponding nilpotent groups, offering a potential method for addressing these classifications.

This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented vehicle data collected in downtown Indianapolis over the course
of 36 driving sessions with various drivers. Each session lasted approximately
20 to 40 minutes. Our primary aim in creating this dataset is to supply the
research community with a diverse and extensive resource for naturalistic
driving data. SceNDD includes a range of driving-related information such as
steering, throttle, brake, and vehicle speed, in addition to environmental
data like road conditions, weather, and GPS information. It can be accessed
at https://github.com/autocntu/SceNDD. In the future, we plan to supplement this
dataset with additional information like vehicle yaw and video data. SceNDD is
compared to existing datasets such as NuScenes and NADS in terms of driving
characteristics, distribution of driving events, and correlations between
instrumented vehicle data. Our analysis reveals promising results that
demonstrate the diversity of driving behaviors captured in this new dataset. A
critical examination of the driving events within SceNDD has also allowed us
to develop a novel taxonomy with four fundamental event types: manuoeuvres,
obstacles, road conditions, and incidents. This taxonomy is expected to
contribute significantly to the research community. Furthermore, we propose
three potential use cases for SceNDD: (1) instrumented vehicle data analysis, (2)
scenario-based driving behavior modeling, and (3) instrumented vehicle team
evaluation. These use cases represent a range of applications for
instrumented vehicle data and have different requirements for data
representation. Finally, we outline additional research directions leveraging
SceNDD and the new event taxonomy presented here. These use cases serve as a
springboard for future research and data collection efforts, and we anticipate
the dataset will continue to evolve in the future. A critical area for future
improvement in SceNDD is the addition of sensory video data, which would
significantly enhance the value of this dataset to the research community. We
intend to supplement SceNDD with video data and explore other forms of
sensory data such as LIDAR. By doing so, SceNDD will become an even more

We are exploring the possibility of reproducing the integral fluctuation theorem (IFT) in a scenario where only a single energy measurement is available. We have developed an expression for the likelihood of observing a specific total energy outcome in this context. Interestingly, this expression is valid for any type of non-projective observation. We have also introduced a modified IFT that applies under these conditions, along with an analysis of its implications for a specific type of system (the driven quantum harmonic oscillator). By comparing our results to simulations, we have found that the IFT remains accurate even in the event of non-Markovian behavior. Furthermore, we have identified a connection between the IFT and the concept of emergent self-correlation, a phenomenon that may be observed in certain quantum systems. We have verified the validity of this connection through simulation and found that it is characterized by an emergent time scale. Our research suggests that the IFT is a robust and universal principle that can provide valuable insights into the behavior of open quantum systems. It is an essential tool that can be used to clarify the subtle mechanisms that govern the transition from microscopic to macroscopic perspectives, including the role of measurement in such transitions. We have demonstrated that the IFT is a single observant-independent principle, thereby resolving any apparent tension with the ideas presented in [Scalise et al., Nat. Phys. 15(6), 211(2019)]. Our analysis also has implications for the understanding of self-correlation in various contexts and may be applied to a range of measurement types beyond the non-Markovian setting explored in [Hemming et al., Phys. Rev. A 99(4), 042126(2019)]. We have validated the IFT through simulation and found that it is accurate for any type of non-projective measurement. We have further discovered that the likelihood of observing certain total energy outcomes can be generalized to a broader class of systems (open quantum channels) under the assumption of weak measurement. We have also found that the implications of the IFT are valid under local observance, connecting it to local self-correlation. Our analysis suggests that the IFT is a reliable tool for analyzing systems (quantum channels) that are in local non-inertia state. We have verified the validity of this conclusion through simulation. Finally, we have generalized the IFT to the level of total energy distributions and found that it yields valuable insights into the self-correlation of systems (the isotropic q-state) that are in local non-inertia state.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and that non-abelian instantons have no deformations that preserve the connection, unless their corresponding 7-dimensional skeletal circle is tangent to the instanton's cohomology class. Additionally, we provide examples of one-dimensional and three-dimensional deformations. Ultimately, applying our methods to the 11-dimension Calabi-Yau manifold with SU(3) holonomy reveals that the structure group can be diminished to SU(2) over a circle-fibered region while maintaining the connection, and that the 3-sphere has the potential to deform into a cone over a torus depending on the cohomology class chosen. Furthermore, by utilizing real Killing spinor methods, we find that non-abelian instantons with a specific cohomology class and a particular 7-dimensional skeletal structure can deform to one another, depending on the instanton's index and the cycle's intersection with the instanton. These findings are expected to be relevant in the study of four-dimensional SU(3) surfaces and K3 surfaces in an eleven-dimension context. We provide explicit descriptions of the relevant structures in the appendices. A cluster of young compact asteroids connected to 39991 Iochroma undergoes a dynamic analysis as part of this study. Our research tests the hypothesis that the Iochroma family's formation can be linked to a specific numerical resonant relationship. To accomplish this, we analyzed the orbital motion of these asteroids under the influence of three distinct resonances: 3:1, 5:2, and 7:2. By conducting 500,000 time-step simulations over 20 million years, starting with 19 members of the Iochroma family, we determined that two of the resonances, 3:1 and 5:2, play a significant role in the orbital evolution of these asteroids. Our findings indicate that the Iochroma family likely originated from an unstable three-body resonance scenario involving these two resonances. A probabilistic assessment of our results suggests that the Iochroma family's formation occurred between 0.84 and 1.23 billion years ago, with a mean age of 0.993 billion years. Moreover, our study confirms that the mean motion resonance relationship between 39991 Iochroma and 1999 OJ4 is not a coincidence. A random sample of 1000 pairs of close pairs first revealed a possible link between the 3:1 resonance and the Iochroma family's age distribution, as 39991 Iochroma and 1999 OJ4 emerged as the pair with the earliest age values. Our research also identifies several distinct scenarios for the origin of the Iochroma family, which is unique compared to other established asteroid families. Additionally, the study proposes a novel method for identifying and ranking existing asteroid families based on their resonance characteristics. By simulating the orbital motion of 1000 close pairs under the influence of the 3:1 mean motion resonance, we obtained a comprehensive dataset that can aid in the identification of resonance relationships among asteroids. Our results indicate that the 3:1 resonance is the most challenging type of mean motion resonance to detect, as only 18 out of 19 members of the Iochroma family showed clear signs of close approaches with 39991 Iochroma. A detailed analysis of the Iochroma family's age distribution, using both itsn and NMLK statistical tools, revealed that the 3:1 resonance and the Iochroma family's age values are not randomly correlated. Our study also provides age correlations for 19 asteroids within the Iochroma family, ranging from 0.83 to 1.

Additionally, we deduce various infinite families of identities comparable to Ramanujan's formula. Furthermore, we investigate the generalizations of these identities to modular forms. This study is an outgrowth of our prior work [Mathematics of Computation, 286, 1-28 (2022)]. The results derived from this study were initially reported at the conference 'Fractal and Complex Dynamics with Applications', held in 2021. The current work specifically focuses on the connections to the modular group, as well as the conclusions to be presented in the follow-up study focus on the cases involving other congruence groups. Our online survey with 235 Signal app users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who are familiar with PINs and those who are not. While 56% of users report using PINs in other applications, only 13% of Signal users changed their PIN from the default one. This low uptake of PINs in Signal is likely due to a lack of understanding among casual users, indicating that the default setup does not adequately protect even enthusiastic users who change their PINs. Furthermore, all these users are susceptible to fingerprint-based PIN retrieval, which could pose a significant security risk to user data, given the increasing prevalence of device-based attacks like ShadowCat. Our findings suggest that users' perceptions of PINs as a security feature are influenced by their level of engagement with the functionality, with Signal developers needing to enhance PINs to support end-to-end encryption and secure backups. By introducing increased recovery obstacles, developers can incentivize users to choose more secure PINs. Our user-centric analysis reveals multiple design opportunities to make PINs a more integral part of the Signal experience. By using PINs to facilitate user-generated backups, developers can shift users' perceptions of PINs from an additional layer of security to an essential component of data preservation. Ultimately, this shift in perspective can help users understand the significance of PINs and increase their adoption in the Signal app.

This significant data rate complicates radio data analysis and necessitates costly computation. To overcome these challenges, LOFAR observations can employ various online analysis tools to streamline the process. REALTA, a pioneering system at the Irish LOFAR station, has successfully demonstrated this capability. Comprising a customized hardware setup and software toolchain, REALTA is poised to expand the scope of online LOFAR observations. In this study, we examine REALTA's hardware and initial observations obtained from the Irish LOFAR. Notably, these online observations are the first to detect radio frequency interference (RFI) and integrate the LOFAR telescope with the Irish National Seismograph Network via a Common Initiative File (CIF) system, enabling co-temporal utility of resources and data analysis. Our results indicate REALTA's capacity for groundbreaking discoveries in areas like RFI mitigation and astrophysical-siesmology at LOFAR scales. REALTA's implementation marks an important milestone in fully utilizing the capabilities of massive radio interferometers. Future plans for the development of a data management system, data distribution channels, and future research goals are also detailed. REALTA's success at the Irish LOFAR serves as an excellent starting point for the advancement of online analysis within the radio interferometer community, with ongoing and future developments of the system at LOFAR's LOFAR-BE data layers and the International LOFAR Workshop on New Frontier Observatories (ILOW-NF) offering opportunities for enhancement and expansion to the entire LOFAR network. voltage dynamics characterization. Ultimately, this work highlights the need for 
integrated frequency and voltage management systems.

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two fundamental models, 
interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings, respectively. Weighed against retrieval accuracy and 
computational efficiency, each has distinct pros and cons. To capitalize on their 
individual strengths, we propose a hybrid framework that synchronizes cross-lingual 
embeddings from both models. To leverage the benefits of synchronous query-document 
embeddings from the interactive model, we propose aligning non-interactive monolingual 
embeddings with their interactive cross-lingual counterparts. We propose a two-stage 
process where unaligned monolingual embeddings are first positioned in a shared space 
as in a non-interactive model, and then, using interactive cross-lingual embeddings as 
anchors, we reposition them. We validate our proposed framework, dubbed AL2IS, on 
datasets including a large web-dataset and smaller datasets DEFT2 and TREC DL datasets. 
Results indicate that in comparison to purely interactive and non-interactive 
approaches, our proposed framework achieves a balanced performance in terms of 
relevance and MRR, retaining 68\% and 69\% of the accuracy and 71\% of the MRR of the 
interactive model, as well as 64\% of the accuracy and 66\% of the MRR of the 
non-interactive model. Furthermore, our framework shows a substantial MRR gain of 9\% 
over non-interactive models with auxiliary data. We also illustrate that our proposed 
framework is scalable, allowing for a balanced performance even when using only a 
portion of the interactive model's query-document cross-lingual embeddings. We 
comprehensively compare the performance of our proposed framework to leading 
cross-lingual information retrieval models, showcasing its potential as a 
retrieval-speed-retrieval-accuracy-optimized model. To facilitate reproduction of 
our findings and provide fair comparisons with other retrieval models, we release 
our code and experiments at https://github.com/behroozz/al2is and the associated 
web-dataset https://github.com/behroozz/crosslingual-web-dataset. The research was

The objective of this study is to examine the concept of betting with quantum characteristics using continuous variables. A betting strategy referred to as Kelly betting is explored, aiming to maximize long-term growth of a gambler's initial stake. To achieve this, a function representing the outcome of a wager is first represented as an operator within the context of quantum theory. Next, the expected value of this operator function, denoted as the quantum spread, is maximized to develop an optimal betting strategy. Both the classical and quantum formulations of the spread are compared, with analysis indicating that the optimal betting strategy can result in increased outcomes under certain conditions. A specific example involving a bet on the momentum of a quantum system is provided, with calculation details shown to demonstrate that the quantum approach to Kelly betting can lead to greater returns in certain scenarios. A detailed analysis of these results is included, with discussion of potential applications and limitations of this betting strategy. Furthermore, the study highlights potential avenues for research into betting strategies with quantum characteristics. A related manuscript is available at arXiv:2112.14249. The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various applications across a wide range of industries, however its real-world adoption has been hindered by serious privacy and fairness concerns. To address these issues, researchers have been exploring the use of fairness metrics and differential privacy in combination with deep learning. A notable approach in this direction is Federated Learning, a method that enables training a universal model across multiple devices while safeguarding sensitive data and promoting fairness. This article provides an overview of recent advancements in this area, covering the integration of fairness and privacy in Federated Learning, and presents a summary of the existing research. Moreover, we delve into the connections between common fairness metrics and the FairSGD model, and we discuss how these concepts can be extended to the Federated Learning setting. Lastly, we touch on the challenges and potential future research directions in this area. This survey aims to equip readers with an in-depth understanding of the intricacies of fairness and privacy in Federated Learning, a topic that has received relatively limited attention in the literature compared to other areas. For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution, $S_{GT}(E',J')$, in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au. This was accompanied by simultaneous gamma ray tracking. The measured relative strength distribution, $S_{GT}(E')$, in the most stable $^{186}$Hg isotope showed significant disagreement with theoretical calculations based on the empirical beta strength function. Instead, data are best described by a different model that uses neighboring isotopes' beta strength to make predictions. To inform model parameters for the $s$-shell nuclei under study, researchers used the Tandy-Engel-Bermondozzi formula to connect $\beta$-strength to nuclear density properties. This was done for $^{106}$Ru, $^{106}$Rh, $^{106}$Pd, and $^{106}$Cd, then applied a nearby-isotopes method to predict $\beta$-strength to $E_{x} \approx -3.5$ MeV in $^{186}$Hg. These predictions closely match the measured strength at this energy, while a notable resonance near $E_{x} \approx 5.5$ MeV may indicate a deformed band in $^{186}$Hg. The research used a total of 135 million beta decays to achieve a 2-sigma significance detection of $S_{GT}(E')$ in the most stable $^{186}$Hg isotope. We explore the intersection of dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified theoretical framework, which includes three right-handed neutrinos, a fermionic dark matter particle, and two additional scalar fields beyond the Standard Model. The interaction between these scalar fields influences both the dark matter relic density and the connection between right-handed neutrinos and dark matter. Our analysis centers around a resonant leptogenesis mechanism that produces baryon asymmetry due to neutrino oscillations, which are facilitated by a non-zero scalar field when one of the scalar fields acquires a vacuum expectation value. Our research demonstrates that the observed relic density of dark matter can be achieved through either the freeze-in production of it or the freeze-out annihilation of it, depending on its interaction with other particles in the theory. We also found cases where the produced dark matter can serve as a source for leptogenesis, which reduces the generated baryon asymmetry if the neutrino-dark matter connection causes lepton-asymmetric neutrino decays. Our analysis delves into various parameter regions that satisfy relic density requirements for both the dark matter candidate and the produced dark matter after leptogenesis starts operating. Our results highlight the significance of the produced dark matter in explaining both the baryon asymmetry and the dark matter observed in our universe. This theoretical framework also evades constraints from laboratory experiments and astronomical observations due to new physics scales that emerge at the TeV scale. Moreover, the produced dark matter candidate, which is referred to as "leptogenesis-induced dark matter," can serve as a model for the previously discovered galactic dark matter halo at Sagittarius A*. Its properties could be tested through future experiments at the Large Hadron Collider and projects for direct dark matter detection. Our analysis also opens the door for potential signatures of dark matter in the cosmic neutrino background, which could be investigated through future experiments. This research introduces a novel concept of "dark matter-induced leptogenesis," which could be explored in depth to further clarify our understanding of dark matter and baryon asymmetry in the universe. It also suggests a new direction for model-building that incorporates both dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified theoretical framework. This theoretical framework could be applied to other phenomena that are not yet fully understood in cosmology and particle physics. Moreover, the produced dark matter candidate could be used as a model for similar, unseen matter that constitutes a substantial portion of our universe. All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and are associated with a specific finite set of integrable field Ward identities. Within Toda conformal field theory framework of $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ type, we derive a precise determination of these identities, which we express through the use of two distinct variables. This identification is based on the existence of $\mathfrak{sl}_3$-type $\hat{\mathfrak{sl}_2}$ loop algebra representations and is consistent with known outcomes for both Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. To facilitate a direct comparison with Toda conformal field theory of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ type, we present a field Ward identity representation that is universally applicable to both $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ and $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ cases. This representation is based on the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$-type Toda conformal field theory's cohomological structure. Furthermore, we also present a precise determination of pre-Ward identities. These identities, in conjunction with known spectral representations, will enable the construction of a universal fermion Fock space for the twisted and untwisted Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ conformal field theories. This, in turn, will serve as the foundation for a comprehensive treatment of Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ conformal field theory's asymptotic fidelity and FZZT transformations. The underlying methodology is equally applicable to Toda conformal field theories of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ type. The untwisted Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ conformal field theory has been used to study a specific class of quantum mechanical supervisors associated with Gauntlett-Stefanski's proposal. The pre-Ward identities and the Fock space for the twisted Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ have also been leveraged in the study of quantum mechanical supervisors proposed by Mazzucato-Stroink-Walker. The untwisted Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ conformal field theory has also been utilized in the study of quantum strings at the AdS$_3\times S^3$ space. The work presented here on Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ has significant implications for a range of string theory-related topics. A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been introduced in the form of Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD). This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity for the phase locking technique. Instead, our method leverages a distinct algorithm to detect phase correlation across two separate light beams transmitted from the sender to the receiver over an extended distance. This algorithm utilizes a data-driven approach based on dynamic tracking of phase correlation. As such, our method eliminates the phase locking challenge by allowing TF-QKD to be implemented without it. In a 1 km fiber trial, our method achieved a secret key rate of 37.5 Mbps with low channel efficiency. This implementation also featured a reduced noise reduction method which enhanced the secret key rate by approximately doubling it in comparison to previous 1 km trials. Moreover, our method demonstrated the capacity for tolerating significant and varying levels of noise over 100 km, reaching a secret key rate of 1 Mbps with a high level of channel efficiency. This method serves as a robust and versatile solution for long-distance and noisy TF-QKD applications, including those in diverse environments and connectivity scenarios. In particular, our method has the potential to be highly suitable for scenarios involving plane-to-plane cross-continent quantum communication applications. In addition to this, our method allows for the implementation of post-processing methods designed to mitigate noise caused by beam instability, potentially further improving performance and achieving maximum secret key rates in various environments and scenarios. This method effectively contributes to the development of practical and efficient quantum communication systems. A related video is available online at the provided link. By employing a crossover training strategy, object detection models are adapted to recognize novel object classes with minimal human intervention. The remarkable achievements of Transformer models in natural language tasks have piqued the interest of computer vision experts to explore their potential applications in visual tasks. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, Transformers rely less on predefined assumptions about data structures, making them more versatile for diverse tasks. As a result, researchers have increasingly applied Transformer models to various computer vision tasks, leading to a rapidly growing body of research. However, the existing literature still lacks an in-depth, comprehensive analysis of these models in the context of computer vision. In this article, we provide an overview of the recent advancements in Transformer models for visual tasks, focusing on key techniques, such as attention, sample processing, and hierarchical structure learning. We also review the latest efforts in applying Transformer models to semantic segmentation, object detection, and other tasks, as well as discussing the unique challenges and opportunities presented by these models in computer vision tasks. Furthermore, we identify the common pitfalls of existing approaches and propose potential research avenues for the computer vision community to adopt and improve on the principles that have driven the success of Transformer models in natural language processing. By adopting a structured and in-depth methodology, we aim to offer a deeper understanding of the state of the art in Transformer-based computer vision tasks, similar to a recent survey on natural language processing. In contrast to existing summaries, our work, focuses on the unique aspects of computer vision tasks, as opposed to generalizations from other areas, such as generative image modeling. Additionally, we explore the potential applications of these models in related visual tasks, such as image captioning, and discuss the critical role of computer vision-specific loss functions in these models. As computer vision experts begin to grasp the principles of Transformer models, we anticipate a more informed and active discussion and exploration of these models in the computer vision community. Importantly, we also acknowledge the potential biases and extra assumptions introduced by these models in computer vision, such as the potential need for pre-trained features and the risk of overfitting, which may limit their performance if not properly addressed. By understanding these trade-offs, the computer vision community can leverage the strengths of these models in a more informed manner. Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions, neglecting the complexities of factor representations. The model's parameterization, though concise, results in inadequate performance in testing environments. We address these limitations by adopting a modern factorization approach called principal component analysis (PCA). This regression-based model, though less mathematically appealing than the classical model, offers superior performance. Two versions of the PCA model, with parameterized factor loadings, are proposed to mimic the classical model's level of detail. The first version maintains time-invariant factor loadings, while the second allows these loadings to evolve over time. We compare the performance of these models, along with the classical Lee-Carter model, to mortality data from six countries, using cross-validation and out-of-sample forecasting techniques as evaluation metrics. The findings indicate that the second PCA model, with time-varying factor loadings, performs better than the classical model and first PCA model in forecasting one to twenty years into the future. However, for long-term forecasting (twenty-one years or more), the first PCA model emerges as the superior option. The motivation behind these models' structures is the expectation that covariates of mortality rates share common, time-varying trends over time, rather than static correlations, which can be better captured by the PCA approach. These models are explored further in a US case study, demonstrating their applicability to diverse data sets. The research suggests that the classical Lee-Carter model may be over-forecasting in the short-term and under-forecasting in the long-term. The proposed PCA models offer balanced forecasting performance across various time horizons. The models' code and data are openly available online. The research indicates that mortality rate factor representations can be better captured by a statistical technique intended for real-valued data, such as PCA, rather than a method like lognormal bivariate hierarchical model targeting joint distributions of adjacent mortality rates and their log-transformed relationships. The models' basing on principal component analysis also enables the interpretation of the obtained factor loadings as weights of relevant covariates, rather than being inherently uninterpretable. The study further examines the PCA models' ability to forecast various types of mortality transitions, such as sharp increases or decreases in mortality rates, as well as changes in mortality patterns from acute to chronic in nature. Cutting-edge neural architecture search (NAS) is heavily reliant on reinforcement learning, but its practical application is restricted by repeated and costly experiments, often resulting in an optimal architecture prediction. We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental group at its boundary. In cases where the fundamental group is finite, we establish precise criteria for it to be virtually cyclic. These findings combine to imply that a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space with a 1-relatively decomposable fundamental group and bounded torsion length must have a finite fundamental group. This result yields finite generation criteria for the fundamental group of certain right-angled Artin groups. Additionally, we demonstrate that if a right-angled graph has a bounded tree-like structure, the corresponding right-angled APPG has a finite fundamental group, leading to the generation of APPGs with diverse properties, including those with a monogenic fundamental group. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an affine manifold with negative curvature does not have a boundary with a finite fundamental group. In addition, under certain boundary conditions on Euler characteristics, we demonstrate that an irreducible CAT(0) space with a fundamental group of finite rank or a bounded torsion length also has a boundary with a finite fundamental group, and this condition is also achievable in the context of right-angled Artin groups. Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an essential process that evaluates how accurately a translation conveys the original text's meaning. Despite its significance, little research exists on developing methods to quantify human translators' levels of expertise and consistency in assessing translation quality. This study investigates whether Bayesian methods can be used to evaluate human translators' ability to provide accurate TQA ratings. We present an approach to determine a translator's level of expertise and consistency by treating TQA ratings as indicators of translations' overall quality. This framework utilizes two types of ratings: a clear and unbiased reference translation provided by a native speaker and a translated text of varying quality for each target language pair. We apply a probabilistic framework to find the parameters that best represent each translator's abilities and compare their performance. This method is tested using data from 30 translators who provided translations and feedback on their quality, which we draw from a platform connecting clients and translators. We also discuss how our approach can be used in a variety of applications, including measuring translator reliability and providing clients with an assessment of translation quality. This study is a starting point for using Bayesian methods to evaluate the reliability of translators and identify reliable translators in a large network of translators. We hope that our research will inspire the development of new methods to quantify translator reliability and facilitate a data-driven approach to Translation Quality Assessment. We plan to make our code and data available to the public, enabling the reproduction of our results and further advancements in this field. Following our initial findings, we have expanded on this research in a subsequent study, which is outlined below. A novel ranking method for translation evaluations is presented, leveraging the expertise and consistency of translators as a unified criterion for assessing translation quality. This approach combines various evaluation metrics into a single, unified standard by utilizing the parameters obtained from the Bayesian assessment. In lotteries with extremely low winning odds, the Ticket Pricing Question remains unresolved: how much should a lottery ticket cost and what should be done with the collected funds? To address this, a model is introduced where the lottery operator's goal is to maximize the expected profit from the ticket's sale. The research considers two scenarios: when the winning odds can be adjusted and when they cannot. Initially, the study focuses on the scenario where the winning odds can be adjusted; here the optimal scenario occurs when the ticket's price is set as the minimum (one unit) to attract as many buyers as possible. In contrast, when the winning odds cannot be adjusted, the ticket's price should be set as high as possible; in a situation with no winning prize, the price should be the maximum the market will bear, while with a non-zero and significant winning prize, the price should be set high enough so that the expected profit from selling the ticket to at least one person covers the cost of the prize in case of a win. An alternative model for the scenario where the winning odds cannot be adjusted is also presented; here the optimal scenario occurs when the ticket's price is set high enough so that the expected profit from selling the ticket to at least two persons covers the cost of the prizes in case of a win. The research also considers various special cases and scenarios, including situations where individual lots may contain multiple winning tickets, and other practical applications. The results obtained are verified using numerical examples. Furthermore, the research focuses on the scenario where the winning odds cannot be adjusted and shows that the ticket's price should be set high enough so that the expected profit from selling the ticket to at least the $\lceil\log_2{m} \rceil$th person covers the cost of the prizes in case the ticket contains $m$ winning tickets, where $\lceil\cdot\rceil$ denotes the ceiling function. Finally, the research focuses on the scenario where the winning odds cannot be adjusted and shows that the ticket's price will be the least common multiple of the numbers from $2^0$ to $m$, where $m$ denotes the number of possible outcomes in the lottery. Our research explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon coupling interaction
affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. We propose a theoretical framework to
calculate the impact of peiophonon coupling, in addition to investigating the role of spatially
static and dynamic deformations in valley switching. Through our analysis, we demonstrate that
piezo-phonon coupling has a significant effect on valley lifetime, showing increased at lower
frequencies and exponentially decreased at higher frequencies. Furthermore, our research
indicates that valley relaxation time is influenced by both static and dynamic deformations but
in opposite ways, with static deformations contributing to slower relaxation and dynamic
deformations contributing to faster relaxation. We show that dynamic deformations account for
over three times faster relaxation rates compared to static deformations. Finally, our study
identifies the rate of elastic relaxation as a critical factor in understanding the behavior of
piezo-phonon coupling and dynamic deformations in two-dimensional materials. We show that
piezo-phonon coupling has a significant effect when the elastic relaxation rate is much slower
than the two-dimensional materials' lattice vibrations, resulting in decreased coupling. On the
other hand, dynamic deformations are more dominant when the elastic relaxation rate is on the
same order or much faster than the two-dimensional materials' lattice vibrations. Throughout
our research, we utilize two-dimensional materials with hexagonal structures such as
h-BN, and MoS2 as test cases to explore the impact of electron-phonon coupling on valley
behavior. Our research identifies peiophonon coupling and dynamic deformations as dominant
interactions in two-dimensional materials, resulting in increased importance to the physical
properties of materials with these interactions. By applying a moderate electric field, the
piezo-phonon coupling interaction in MoS2 can be enhanced. Our research also demonstrates that
dynamic deformations can be amplified by using a mechanical force, resulting in increased
dominance of dynamic deformations over piezo-phonon coupling in two-dimensional materials.

The VisDA 2022 Challenge aims to achieve unsupervised adaptation in deep neural networks, adapting a network trained on a known set of classes, often referred to as the source domain, to an unseen but related domain. This challenge focuses on a unique problem where the source and target domains have different sets of classes. This is addressed through a network designed to retain its original class boundaries while adapting to new data from a target domain, often with additional classes not present in the source domain. This problem is further complicated by the fact that the target domain features are available during training. To tackle this problem, our T2DA architecture, based on two normalisation layers with a shared weight, uses a simple yet efficient technique to remove the source domain bias present in feature maps. This is done by introducing a bias term estimated through a moving average of the target domain mean feature values. Our solution also involves a novel loss function that minimises the influence of source domain data by measuring the distance between feature maps of the same class. This is based on a histogram-based metric that takes into account the class distribution. Our solution further enhances its performance using an ensemble technique, by aggregating predictions from multiple networks, each trained on different target domain datasets with varying numbers of classes, to tackle scenarios where the target domain features may contain noisy data. This ensemble technique also involves selecting optimal data points to train on from the target domain, based on a measure of class distribution. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our solution across three datasets, with a notable improvement in adaptation accuracy compared to other state-of-the-art techniques, especially when dealing with large datasets. Visualisation experiments also indicate that the source domain bias is effectively removed, and the network adapts to the target domain with high accuracy. t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently. Utilizing an iterative procedure, it achieves more effective embeddings than the conventional t-SNE method when working with such data types, as shown through its simulation on sample datasets. Furthermore, this algorithm proves its value in embedding neural network features, a feat not easily achievable with t-SNE. Notably, it is highly compatible with t-SNE and can be easily incorporated into existing software for enhanced performance on spherical data. Ultimately, this algorithm presents a significant improvement for visualizing data that follows a von Mises-Fisher distribution, such as surfaces and closed manifolds. As a result, it has far-reaching implications for researchers working to embed spherical data in a lower-dimensional format. Its source code is also made available for potential use. In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. This method is well-suited for simulating complex many-body systems, particularly with large numbers of qubits, as it simplifies the experimental procedure and reduces the complexity of control techniques. This research focuses on the digital-analog simulation of second-order fermionic Hamiltonians, and we've developed a novel class of digital-analog algorithms for this purpose. We've also proposed a specific distribution of quantum computing resources, divided between digital and analog components, and demonstrated that the hybrid model can match or improve upon analog quantum simulators in terms of required precision, often with a significant reduction in qubit count. This research also illustrates a strategy for translating algorithms designed for digital quantum computers to simulate analog quantum systems, and shows that digital-analog computing offers an efficient compromise between analog and digital quantum computing models. A critical aspect of this research is the simulation of fermionic systems using fermionic mode conversion, and we've developed a method for this purpose. This method is based on a quantum version of the Schwinger-Dyson equation and is applicable to fermionic systems with arbitrary dimension. This approach also allows for the generalization of fermionic mode conversion in Kitaev models with non-abitary lattice symmetries. This research also includes a simulation of a model for superconducting circuits with fermionic mode conversion and demonstrates the feasibility of analog digital approach to quantum computing. The research includes a detailed analysis of quantum computing errors and shows that digital-analog computing offers an efficient trade-off between control complexity and control precision. A related quantum software package, called digital-analog.py, has been developed to support the digital-analog approach and is publicly available. This package includes functions for fermionic mode conversion, fermionic hopping, fermionic creation and annihilation operators, and quantum circuit construction, and demonstrates the digital-analog quantum computing protocol. Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to develop algebraic formulas describing various graph characteristics and encoding multiple graph invariants through their evaluation processes. Certain graphs, including complete and bipartite structures, can be identified by analyzing the properties of polynomials derived from them. In general, graph polynomials are categorized as holonomic, implying that the coefficients within their expansion, when evaluated at -q (for q > 0), result in a finite sequence. This work explores a theoretical framework for understanding the graph polynomial coefficients. Specifically, we establish a recursive formula applicable to a broad class of graph polynomials, including the Cayley-Hadamard transform of polynomials. This transformation allows for encoding multiple graph invariants within a single polynomial invariant. In addition, we provide examples of complete and bipartite graphs, illustrate the connection between their polynomials and chromatic and partition functions. These findings converge towards a central question: What graph polynomials' coefficients give rise to a partition function describing a one-dimensional lattice? The answer to this, in turn, may unveil the underlying query: What graph invariants define a one-dimensional lattice? This work aims to introduce a novel approach for encoding invariants of graphs on a linear array and identifies recursive formulas for evaluating this encoding. Ultimately, we propose a framework for understanding the encoding of various graph invariants and offer a possible interpretation: The partition function describes an interacting Fermion model on a one-dimensional lattice. Moreover, related concepts and findings are also explored.

* They propose a novel approach for understanding the encoding of interacting Fermion models on a one-dimensional lattice using graph polynomials evaluated at -q (for q > 0).
* They provide a possible interpretation: The partition function describes an interacting Fermion model on a one-dimensional lattice.
* They relate concepts and findings to quantum field theories and lattice models.

To guarantee matching among all agents, the Deferred Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that stable matchings are achieved even with shorter, albeit incomplete, preference lists, thus sparking curiosity as to why and how agents should optimize these lists for the best possible matches. Researchers have explored this question in a theoretical model introduced by Birg and Klaus, which we extend by allowing agents to adapt their preference lists over time. Our findings, based on experiments with both synthetic and real-world data from the UK residency matching program, reveal that there are strategies for updating preference lists that consistently outperform the baseline of consistently updating all preferences or maintaining a fixed list. These strategies can be generalized to various related problems. Furthermore, using data from the US National Resident Matching Program, we provide empirical support for the effectiveness of one such strategy, at the same time highlighting the trade-offs between the quality of matches and the level of preference information. Our findings suggest that incentives for updating preference lists arise when there is a significant gap between the actual and optimal matches in a given iteration of the matching process. Overall, our results demonstrate that matching algorithms can be designed to take into account the interplay between the level of preference information and the adaptability of agents, thus enabling improved outcomes when adapted correctly. These insights could potentially lead to new applications in a broader setting where agents adapt their preference lists over time. Moreover, our research reveals that while preference information plays a crucial role in achieving stable matches, the level of preference information does not directly impact the stability of matches, a finding that is consistent with empirical data from both the US and UK programs. To this end, we suggest that agents, particularly in the residency matching programs, should be provided an opportunity to share their perspectives and adapt their preference lists accordingly, at the same time as matching algorithms are designed with the level of preference information in mind. This has led us to develop a novel fusion framework, named BEVFusion, where LiDAR features and bevy of camera frames are used in conjunction. Experimental results on the NuScenes dataset have shown that our method surpasses the existing state-of-the-art object detection techniques. Furthermore, we've found that LiDAR data is indispensable during camera failures and that our method outperforms existing fusion approaches by a considerable margin. Ultimately, our work on BEVFusion has provided a resilient and efficient framework for 3D object detection, even in the event of camera failures. A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural models holds great promise, but these models have a significant drawback: they can only express what they've seen during training. However, this limitation is particularly problematic when translating English to SPARQL, because questions often involve variables, but also frequently include constraints such as variable variable equality or range constraints on variables. Previous approaches attempted to address this issue either by training on a vast number of possible variables or by hard-coding range constraints into the translation. Our research takes a different approach by developing a copy mechanism that allows SPARQL machine translation models to generate constraint expressions related to variables that have not been encountered during training. Our proposed mechanism is compatible with various neural models with self-attention. We test its effectiveness using two datasets, BioKB and WebSPARQL, and found that it significantly improves the precision of translations, particularly when translating complex queries with variable variable equality constraints. Our results also show that our approach can learn general equalities without being hard-coded, which was not possible with the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our technique is not limited to SPARQL machine translation and can be applied to other language translation tasks as well. Our research is the first to address this specific issue in SPARQL machine translation and presents a novel technique, which is not a part of any existing state-of-the-art SPARQL machine translation method. Our evaluation also distinguishes our approach from existing state-of-the-art SPARQL machine translation methods on two datasets, BioKB and WebSPARQL. Our research is further validated by crowdsourcing, which confirms that our approach produces more accurate translations compared to state-of-the-art SPARQL machine translation models. This study introduces a novel approach to hierarchical clustering, drawing from the mathematical fields of category theory and algebraic geometry. The proposed method centers on a functorial interpretation of the average linkage clustering algorithm, utilizing a simple and robust method to resolve overlap issues. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world data sets, including human cancer samples, demonstrate the superiority of this functorial approach over traditional average linkage clustering when dealing with overlapping cases. Furthermore, the functorial method is shown to maintain consistency across multiple runs, making it a reliable tool for comparative analyses. Additionally, the study provides a systematic comparison between functorial and average linkage clustering results. Finally, the proposed approach is incorporated into a new tool, known as FUNCLUST, which enables users to leverage hierarchical clustering in a more robust and reliable manner, especially when dealing with overlapping cases. FUNCLUST combines the functionality of three widely used clustering tools, allowing for the automatic application of the functorial method in clustering workflows. In particular, the tool is compatible with ClusterPicker, a popular tool for analyzing human cancer data at the clinic. The integration of FUNCLUST's new functionality with existing tools on the CoCoMac platform enables seamless deployment of the functorial method in clinical settings. Ultimately, the study's results demonstrate the functorial method's superiority over average linkage clustering when dealing with overlapping cases. Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors, a common pattern in real-world data. This problem is particularly relevant in streaming data, where incorporating a learning-based method can enhance predictive performance. This research introduces a streaming tensor completion approach based on tensor completion and learning, utilizing a Patch Tracking mechanism to adaptively select and update low-rank subsystems. By leveraging a more robust and efficient evaluation function, the method can complete tensors while maintaining low computational complexity. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method performs better on video data when compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the approach is complex-efficient and adaptable to various data recovery tasks. Additionally, the method's code and experimental datasets are openly available for the community to evaluate its performance. This research makes two key contributions: a novel and efficient algorithm for completing streaming tensors and a framework for learning-based tensor completion. Recent findings have highlighted the prevalence of magnetically active flare stars that host corona regions and support type II radio beams originating from their upper atmospheres. Our observation of CR Draconis, a flare star binary system with a period of 1.84 days, involved monitoring radio activity at 3.05 MHz for nearly five years using the GREEN radio receiver. The data showed consistent and persistent radio emission with minimal intensity variations, amounting to 0.2 kHz, throughout the observation period. Although intensity fluctuations were small, spectral drift of about 1.6 kHz per day took place during the entire monitoring period. We deduce that low-frequency emission stems from an electron-cyclotron maser induced by a coherent beam of plasma mode electrons originating from the star's corona. The observed radio emission was consistent with a two-component spectrum consisting of a flat plateau and a steepening slope. The former was attributed to a circularly polarized spot, while the latter to a pair of opposite spots. Analysis of long-term data revealed a periodic pattern in CR Draconis' radio emission that correlated with the binary system's 1.84-day orbital cycle. More interestingly, in some instances, the periodic pattern was overlaid with a 12.8-day beat period superimposed on a sideband. In recent years, neural rendering techniques have revolutionized the approach to rendering virtual scenes, significantly surpassing traditional methods in terms of realism and detail. However, when it comes to rendering virtual human avatars, these techniques prove inadequate for capturing the complexities of a human body. This becomes particularly problematic when it comes to deriving downstream applications such as metaverse interactions, physiological research, and game applications. To address this limitation, we propose an articulated neural rendering framework that synchronizes a neural renderer with a rigid body simulation of a character's skeleton. This integration allows the renderer to compute vertex positions based on the optimized bone weights obtained from the body simulation. By combining these two components with a high-resolution neural texture, we create the foundation for a realistic and coherent view of a virtual human from any angle. To ensure seamless synthesis of the rendered view, we develop a novel editor for editing neural textures, leveraging user-provided real-world reference images to merge with user-drawn overlay images. This merged texture serves as input to our high-fidelity neural renderer, which generates photorealistic images of virtual human avatars under various poses and rotations. Our results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing state-of-the-art methods, showcasing impressive advancements in the quality of avatar images. Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) have achieved remarkable accuracy in image classification tasks, even when evaluating distorted or manipulated images. However, from a human perspective, these transformations are often unreasonable and result in significant changes to the visual appearance of images. To investigate this discrepancy between human and ANN perception, we designed an experimental study to gauge human preferences and classification performance in relation to various image transformations across different levels of intensity. Our findings reveal that ANNs are equally proficient, but sometimes hindered by minor changes, while humans exhibit greater adaptability and tend to prefer moderate transformations. Emphasizing the diversity between human and ANN perception, we highlight the benefits and limitations of these discrepancies and propose novel applications for ANNs in image processing. To facilitate future research, we make our dataset and evaluation tools publicly available to facilitate access. Additionally, we provide a complementary analysis through Annexes, including raw data, to enable researchers to expand upon our work. Specifically, we note that our study focuses on image transformations rather than specific objects, distinguishing it from studies on misclassification and when algorithms outperform humans. Similarly, we study ANNs under natural (normal) conditions to distinguish our work from studies on adversarial attacks that intentionally manipulate images to mislead ANNs. Given these key distinctions, we anticipate that our study will appeal to researchers working on visual recognition, particularly those focused on understanding human preferences and ANN limitations from a transformation perspective, rather than specific objects. We apply this simulation method to the Kitaev and $Z_2$ XY model trimer compounds, such as $\alpha$-NaYbO$_2$ and its analogues, providing a comparative analysis with existing quantum experiments and theoretical models. We also explore the influence of intercluster connections, observed in the recent synthesis $\alpha$-NaYbO$_2$(Pt$_4$)(OH)$_2$(${\rm Yb}^{\rm III}$)$_2$Br$_6$.2D-H$_3$PW$_12$O$_4$ and the related Kitaev model analogue BaPt$_4$Si$_6$O$_{20}$, characterized by a planar ring structure linking eight spin clusters. We found that the trimer-based quantum Monte Carlo approach exhibits excellent agreement with exact solutions on smaller clusters, while its application to materials-based simulations shows that the observed magnetic susceptibility and specific heat behaviors can be accurately explained within a scenario of loosely coupled spin clusters, with temperatures defining the crossover from individual cluster physics to collective behavior estimated to be around 4--5 K. Furthermore, our simulation reveals a dominance of cluster-dimer interactions over cluster-cluster interactions in the relevant temperature regime. We also identified a numerical disagreement between our simulation results and existing analytical model for the specific case of the Kitaev model, with the observed magnetic susceptibility not matching the predicted linear dependence on temperature at low temperatures. Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-variant models, have demonstrated the ability to perform zero-shot learning by leveraging pre-existing text data to predict unseen inputs. To facilitate this learning, additional text can be provided as input to fine-tune pre-trained language models for specific tasks, a process known as meta-tuning. To streamline this process, a dataset collection of meta-tuned models, including GPT-7 and GPT-33 million parameters, has been developed and made publicly available. This collection can be used in conjunction with natural language prompts to fine-tune pre-trained language models for a variety of tasks without the need for annotated data. Furthermore, this paper explores the impact of model and dataset composition, as well as prompt composition, to maximize zero-shot learning performance. Results indicate that a well-curated collection of pre-trained models and datasets can achieve state-of-the-art performance on a diverse set of tasks, including sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and question answering, based on human evaluations. To facilitate adaptation and replication, this collection, known as BigZilu, is publicly available along with BigZilu-Tools, a C++-based command-line interface for easily fine-tuning and deploying meta-tuned models from the collection, and the CodeCrawler repository, a dataset collection of code snippets and natural language prompts to facilitate replication and adaptation. Analysis of the collection reveals that a subset of seven models, each with approximately 7 million parameters, can collectively match the performance of a much larger model, including a 135 million parameter GPT-5 model, on a diverse set of tasks. Moreover, this collection highlights the importance of dataset and prompt composition to maximize zero-shot learning performance. To facilitate the identification of task-agnostic features, a tool known as CodeCrawler is used to analyze the prompt and code similarity between tasks. This analysis enables the identification of a subset of 380 prompts, approximately 7% of the total, that collectively maximize zero-shot learning performance. Furthermore, this collection highlights the importance of dataset and prompt composition to maximize zero-shot learning performance. As a result of this collection, a dataset of 1,000 natural language prompts and corresponding code snippets known as CodePron is made publicly available. This collection enables the identification of task-agnostic features that can be used to facilitate zero-shot learning. Results indicate that a model meta-tuned on CodePron achieves a 0.848 recall value while also achieving a 0.846 F1-score on the SST-2 dataset

Our methodology involves evaluating the effectiveness of diverse millimeter and submillimeter observational methods in measuring spectroscopic redshifts and optimizes future observations to maximize the proportion of robust redshifts obtained. To facilitate this process, a publicly accessible code is shared at (https://github.com/tgwilliams/redshift-finding-chromatic-numbers). Our analysis includes a comprehensive study of 41 spectroscopically confirmed galaxies at redshifts z >= 1 that have been observed in the millimeter and submillimeter spectrum, as well as 41 randomly selected galaxies from the same survey with unknown redshifts. Our results are further compared against over 800 galaxies from the SDSS-II dataset that have known redshifts. By comparing the H30α SFR with IRAC and Hα SFRs, the H30α SFRs are found to be consistently 0.1 mag more sensitive to the SFR than IRAC measurements but 0.5 mag less sensitive than Hα measurements, with the H30α SFR indicating the presence of a 0.7 mag offset in the IRAC and Hα SFRs. Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear epidemic models, which are inherently non-autonomous and partially unknown. To address these issues, a novel Lyapunov design approach is developed, leveraging a tailored Lyapunov function candidate and gain adaptation. This allows the observer to converge to the system's state under certain mild conditions and provides a theoretical framework for its analysis. To validate these findings, a numerical example is performed, demonstrating the proposed observer's ability to converge under various conditions. Furthermore, a SIR model is analyzed in the presence of unknown parameters, and an adaptive gain design is developed to overcome this challenge. This results in a theoretically justifiable observer that achieves convergence under milder observability conditions. Ultimately, these designs are evaluated through simulation and testing. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications using these graphs. This is particularly the case for link prediction tasks, where current model static approaches fall short, and more advanced two-stream models often compromise on efficiency for more accurate results. To find a middle ground, we suggest a universal adaptation strategy for static models to accommodate temporal knowledge graphs, and assess its efficacy in comparison to two-stream models on a wide range of benchmark datasets. We demonstrate that static models can be modified to achieve results comparable to more complex models, and even outperform them in some cases when speed is a priority. This discovery implies that static models should be the first choice when considering the development of temporal knowledge graphs. Inspired by this finding, we introduce BEXPE, a novel static model that outperforms existing solutions in link prediction and provides universal adaptation capabilities. We make the code and models for our main results available. Additionally, a companion repository contains extra results, including models for the Knowledge Graph Link Prediction Shared Task 2022. This repository also contains a tutorial on embedding static knowledge graphs.

We have introduced a method for constructing cone decompositions over expander graphs, which can be used to create several types of high-dimensional dimension expanders. These dimension expanders come in two forms - simple and weighted - and can be constructed by wrapping the given graph's cover with a suitable quotient. This method allows us to build the first known family of bipartite high-dimensional expanders in dimensions greater than 1. To establish the correctness of this method, we proved that graphs resulting from wrapping covers of expander graphs possess both strong expansion and a small O(log n) dimensional space. Furthermore, we discovered that graphs resulting from wrapping covers of bipartite expander graphs possess a symmetric strong dimensional property. This method allows us to achieve a significant breakthrough by independently constructing bipartite expander graphs of dimension 2 and weight 2 from first principles. This was previously an open problem, solved by our innovative algorithm which generates these graphs directly. Our algorithm demonstrates that in a random bipartite graph on n vertices and edges m, there exists a subset of size O(log n) with an extremely high probability that the induced subgraph is both bipartite and an expander. This result is achieved by simply selecting the specified subset from the given graph. These expander graphs and the novel algorithm using random sampling have far-reaching implications. This joint contribution is part of ongoing research in high-dimensional dimension expanders."

Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe complications, and mental health professionals recognize social media posts as valuable indicators. However, gathering related data typically requires significant time, effort, and resources, and making mistakes during data collection can undermine the accuracy of analytics results. In this research, we developed a data set called DepDepAcad, which includes 1,570 social media entries from users with acute depression and 19,464 entries from healthy users. Our study included an empirical analysis of DepDepAcad's composition, which aided in a more precise classification of depression from social media content. Our experiments with six different machine learning algorithms on DepDepAcad revealed that Ensemble has demonstrated the best performance so far, and we plan to continuously expand the data set to support more advanced depression detection capabilities. The data set and code are available on GitHub at https://github.com/ResearchITLM/DepDepAcad.

We've developed two probabilistic models for the COVID-19 pandemic. We've derived the statistical properties of these models, including correlation functions and probability distributions. These models, which build on existing work and take into account the rapid variations in infection rates, can be used to predict future trends and provide accurate error estimates. This allows healthcare officials to make more informed decisions regarding hospital resource allocation and whether new measures are needed to prevent the hospital from becoming overwhelmed. We've applied the models to data from the United States, finding that the initial model, which assumes constant infection rates, closely matches the actual data, while the model that incorporates fluctuations is too extreme to match the data. However, if a correlation function with the correct average is applied to the actual data, it significantly improves the match. This suggests that the initial model is the most accurate representation of the data. We've also found that the models are stationarily stable, meaning that long-term trends are consistent. This provides a reliable basis for decision-making. We've verified our results by performing multiple independent analyses, in addition to performing checks for errors. We've further validated our results by applying them to two different datasets and obtaining similar outcomes. This provides a level of consistency and confidence in our findings. Finally, we acknowledge that the models do not capture the full complexity of the pandemic, but we believe that they provide a simple and effective solution to modeling COVID-19. As the pandemic continues to evolve, we anticipate being able to apply our models to anticipate future COVID-19 developments. Future work could involve incorporating additional factors, such as the effects of vaccination and changes in human behavior.
