Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery bounds for a wide range of such problems. Specifically, we address the case of estimating a matrix of rank one that may have varying levels of noise across different groups of entries. This scenario encompasses several real-world applications including regression problems with unevenly spaced data and graph signal recovery with unknown noise patterns. Initially, we will establish the optimal rate of convergence for estimating matrix parameters under squared-loss objective in a model with group-wise heteroskedastic noise. This will be based on two key conditions that define the geometry of the data, one of which is a version of the weak restricted isometry property tailored to group-wise heteroskedastic noise. The other condition concerns the diagonalizability of data features and is essential for achieving optimal convergence rates. The obtained results are then extended to regression problems with unevenly spaced data, while methods for numerical computation are provided, including an analysis of the sample size requirements for such scenarios. Furthermore, we will generalize the obtained results to the case of multi-dimensional matrix recovery issues. The methods for numerical computation will be based on convex optimization techniques with optimal objective function values being certified both in noise and out. This will be achieved by using the strong convexity of the objective function, along with a characterization of the optimal point that minimizes the data fitting term while controlling the excess risk. The obtained results for the rank-one matrix estimation problem are then generalized to the case of low-rank matrix recovery issues. The primary distinction in this case lies in the fact that the geometric conditions that define the structure of data features can be satisfied only in the average sense and not in the group-wise setting. Consequently, we will establish sub-optimality gaps for the low-rank matrix recovery issue and provide certification of the sample size requirements for the recovery issue. Moreover, we will establish tighter sample size requirements for the linear regression problem with uniformly distributed data entries than those obtained under group-wise heteroskedastic noise setting. The methods for numerical computation will be based on the use of random design convex optimization techniques with a certificate of the optimal objective function values being obtained both in noise and out. This combined observable enhances the sensitivity to new physics beyond the Standard Model, especially in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at a B-meson collider. We calculate $R_\Sigma$ using the soft photon correction to the inclusive $R^{\ell'}_K$ ratio at B factories and find that in the Standard Model, $R_\Sigma$ is slightly lower than $R_K$ by about 0.003%. New physics scenarios with non-universal couplings or photon exchange boost the $\sigma(S_{4\ell'}\cos^2\theta_\ell)$ asymmetry, making $R_\Sigma$ more sensitive than $R_K$ in that case. We outline a method to measure $R_\Sigma$ at Belle-II and BELLE, aiming to achieve a precision of about 0.75% and 0.43%, respectively. This proposed measurement can be completed with data from 2022 to 2024, reaching a 0.0% precision, three standard deviations from null if no new physics exists. Furthermore, $R_\Sigma$ can be measured with Belle-II and BELLE with data from 2022 to 2034, reaching a precision of about $2.6\cdot10^{-3}$ and $1.3\cdot10^{-3}$ respectively, three standard deviations from null if no new physics exists. We outline a plan for a more precise measurement at Super-BELLE with data from 2022 to 2034, reaching a precision of about $5\cdot10^{-5}$. This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is effectively "plug-and-play" capable, meaning it can effectively regulate the system even if all other agents disconnect. Building on prior work by Zeng and Tsiotras, we employ passivity and graph robustness principles to develop robustly stable and robustly stable designs for general and single-input systems, respectively. In single-input systems, we take it further by creating controllers that can tolerate disconnected agents and passivity-based controllers that can effectively regulate systems with randomly fluctuating link failures. To validate our approach, we also develop practical designs for systems with multiple inputs. Experimental results using quadcopter arrangements demonstrate that our designs can be practical and effective in real-world applications. Notably, the developed output-feedback controllers are highly decentralized, meaning they do not require agents to have complete system information, only their immediate neighbors. This property makes these controllers highly scalable for systems with large numbers of interconnected agents. This study's contributions are significant because it is the first to achieve scalable output-feedback controller designs with "plug-and-play" capabilities for general multi-channel systems, improving previous decentralized controller designs which required complete system knowledge. This study's findings are extensively validated through various real-world experiments, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed approaches. One of the key findings is that passivity-based distributed control designs with "plug-and-play" capabilities are generally not possible for general multi-channel systems, emphasizing the need for more complex controller design methods, as demonstrated in this study. Additionally, we take a step further by developing output-feedback controller designs with "plug-and-play" capabilities for single-input systems, representing a previously underexplored research area. This study's findings are expected to have a significant impact on the research community by providing valuable design approaches for large-scale multi-agent systems, as well as promoting the application of passivity-based controller design methods to tackle distributed control challenges. Moreover, we take a practical approach to designing controllers by leveraging passivity-based design principles to develop scalable distributed controllers with "plug-and-play" capabilities, which can effectively tolerate various types of link failures, as demonstrated in this study. This study's approach is expected to be highly valuable for real-world controller design applications due to its scalability and robustness properties. We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on randomly sampled CT image segments, and then, by treating the feature extraction as a new modality, we incorporate information from the entire scan while adding a secondary BERT instance for combined spatial and temporal feature fusion. The combined features are subsequently fed into a fully-connected layer for classification, and our approach is successfully applied to the diagnosis of a diverse patient cohort, including individuals with contrasting imaging characteristics. By leveraging double feature extraction, we enhance the model's expressiveness and achieve competitive performance with improved robustness to rare diseases through experimentation on four diverse datasets. The resulting system demonstrates a high degree of versatility, and our source code is publicly available on GitHub. When tested on an unseen dataset consisting of Spanish-speaking individuals, we achieve superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art models, and our approach demonstrates satisfactory translation-resistant properties. Moreover, when evaluated across various ethnic groups, our model exhibits favorable performance, and our bit-by-bit analysis suggests that the model lacks bias in its decision-making process, and our study highlights the importance of data quality in medical AI systems. Ultimately, our approach successfully applies transfer learning while avoiding biases related to race, language, and ethnicity. This highly interdisciplinary field, at the intersection of physics, biology, sociology, and computer science, analyzes the intricate relationships between entities to reveal patterns that would be lost in individual data. Recently, a significant amount of network collections have become available through massive information flows like online publications, datasets, and code repositories, waiting to be tapped by researchers. However, navigating this vast landscape of available research can be overwhelming, especially for those new to network science. A decentralized exchange known as a DEX enables users to make transactions without relying on an external party, thanks to the use of smart contracts. The DEX market, which is primarily based on blockchain technology, has experienced rapid growth driven by the proliferation of new blockchain projects. A DEX transaction involves two key components: the cost associated with operating the blockchain and the fee paid to a blockchain 'validator' for verifying the transaction.  Due to the variability in verification fees charged by different blockchains, some DEXs face volatility in their operating costs which can be a major turn-off for potential users. Our paper examines the economic dynamics of DEXs by modeling a scenario where potential users adopt a strategy of choosing the DEX with the lowest operating costs at any given point in time. As a result, the market equilibrium price is theoretically identified as a geometric mean of variables including variable transaction fees, token values, and blockchain operating costs. The analysis also sheds light on the factors that contribute to the likelihood of a DEX's operating costs becoming unstable. The findings are substantiated by experiments using data from 81 DEXs operating across 7 different blockchains. 

The research findings indicate that a DEX's operating costs are likely to be unstable if it processes a large number of transactions and has a large total value of assets being traded. Moreover, a DEX's probability of success is inversely correlated with the number of existing DEXs on a given blockchain and appears to be influenced by a complex relationship between the frequency of new blockchain projects and DEX adoption rates. 

Ultimately, the research suggests that a DEX should prioritize token listing strategies that focus on balancing liquidity, token popularity, and market demand to minimize the risk of unstable operating costs. 

The research's conclusions can be extended to other decentralized applications that operate on blockchains.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. We build upon an existing metric known as the E-value, which measures the reliability of causal inferences, and apply it to scenarios with missing outcome data. Through case studies on Facebook's partially-observed conversion events, we develop an approach to conduct large-scale sensitivity analysis by contributing three key improvements. Firstly, we develop a Bayesian estimation technique for sensitivity parameters using unreliable benchmarks; secondly, we establish a statistical method for determining the optimal range of parameter values; and thirdly, we outline an efficient procedure for performing an extensive number of analyses. We also compare and distinguish our approach from existing methods for recovering missing data, such as multiple imputation and regression estimation. Through a large-scale code review, we found that while Python cryptographic interfaces are generally provided by established third-party libraries, the majority of applications do not utilize these libraries, instead opting for lower-level, inbuilt cryptographic functions. This check list can also be applied to other programming languages to help identify and mitigate potential misuses. By performing code reviews, new developers can ensure that they adhere to secure best practices from the outset. We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with enhanced resolution. To achieve this, we introduce a novel deep learning-based model called NuSPAN, which is distinct from existing sparse models that assume uniform sparsity across all signals. NuSPAN is characterized by its ability to learn nonuniform sparse groupings both vertically and horizontally through proximal network layers. A weighted Proximal Average Network layer enables the model to learn and apply diverse weights to group-wise connections, while a Sample Grouping Layer allows for flexible assignment of data samples to various groups. By iterating the sampling and grouping process, NuSPAN is able to identify and tackle intricate sparse patterns. To train NuSPAN, we incorporate a dual approach that converts the optimization problem into a matching network training task. A pre-trained NuSPAN model is then applied to a seismic data set for reflection coefficient estimation as part of a two-stage seismic inversion process. For high-resolution enhancement, we introduce a sequential iteration strategy that involves iteratively adding the output of the previous iteration to the input of the current iteration. Our numerical results demonstrate NuSPAN's ability to accurately estimate the reflection coefficients even at extremely low sampling rates and minor modulation depths, while its model size is determined by the number of group-wise connections, not by the size of the signals. As a result, NuSPAN is capable of handling large-scale seismic data sets with various input sizes and group counts, and its model can be further improved using ensemble learning techniques to achieve even better outcomes. Moreover, NuSPAN's applicability is not limited to seismic reflection inversion, as it can be applied to a broad range of sparse signal deconvolution problems in fields such as image processing, gene selection, and others. We believe that NuSPAN has the potential to be a versatile model for sparse signal processing in diverse domains. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. However, POS annotators seek more than 90% accuracy in contemporary standard languages. We argue that accurate POS annotation for historical languages, often accompanied by numerous ambiguities, can benefit from a different approach. Instead of assigning a single tag to a word, a set of valid tags is considered. This method has been tested on Middle English, specifically 15th-century texts known as Early Modern English, showing improved results over single-tag annotation. A significant advantage of this technique is its enhanced robustness against data scarcity, common in historical corpora. We also observed reduced overfitting when annotating the first Middle English text from 1395 in Middle English and found that valence features do not necessarily correlate with desired accuracy. A comprehensive evaluation of this technique has been conducted on 17th-century English texts from CoraC. Results indicate a substantial accuracy gain, up to 16.7%, and a significant reduction in expected errors compared to standard single-tag annotation. Furthermore, POS tagging with a set of valid tags allows for automatic correction of machine learning-based single-tag annotation, leading to a 50% or higher correction rate, with no notable difference between the correction methods. Interestingly, while the standard approach produces accurate results for standard English from 17th century, the set-valued method demonstrates its value in historical corpora, such as CoraC, by accurately tagging words that previous methods had labeled as unknown. This method has been successfully applied to annotate the first Middle English text from 1395 in Middle English. Good quality requirements management is crucial for successful city service development, and increased stakeholder involvement creates new challenges for requirement managers.
  They now face tasks like prioritizing diverse stakeholder needs, and ensuring that services meet these varied requirements while adhering to common standards and regulations.
This paper presents an innovative system that aids requirement managers in translating city demands into formal specifications for smart services development.
Our intelligent assistant is designed to be particularly useful for non-technical city officials, providing an user-friendly platform to describe requirements and obtain suitable smart services solutions.
It also produces an accurate formal specification as input for software developers to create the desired smart services.
Our system's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application in two real-world smart services. 
A formal evaluation of its key components was conducted and made available on IEEE's Repository as two independent evidence papers. 
We further provide an educational course to train future smart city requirement managers in using our assistance tool effectively. 
All course materials, formal specifications, and other supporting materials are freely available online at requirementsmart.city. 
In addition to English, our system is available in Russian at smartrequirements.ru.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn (2009), we analyze and predict the extreme joint behavior of wind, wave height, and wind speed at Helgoland Sea Station, a location in the North Sea, where severe storms occur frequently. To achieve this, we fit a multivariate extreme value model to an original time series by transforming it into a standardized series and fitting a spatial regression. Our model accounts for dependence between variables using a spatial copula and for non-stationary extreme sea states by including a dynamic memory period. Estimation is conducted through local likelihood optimization, and forecasting is facilitated by generating synthetic paths from the conditional model. Focusing on ocean environments, our model can be used to simulate joint spatial distributions during storms and assess their conditional extremes in advance. The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is undergoing significant transformation.  Given the regulatory constraints of working with DICOM data, there is a notable scarcity of accessible datasets and comprehensive tooling.  We introduce highdicom, a publicly accessible Python library aimed at making DICOM data and the communications protocols surrounding it easily usable, while also providing functionality for converting data into other formats.  This tool supports reading and writing various DICOM data formats, including those with multi-dimensional numerical image data, as well as providing a simple way to classify such data with Python's PyTorch.  We also provide examples of working with datasets in major machine learning libraries, including OpenSlide for image preprocessing and the ANONIES tool for anonymizing dataset and DICOM files.  Furthermore, we introduce MDQ, a publicly accessible dataset derived from the Brats18 challenge, which is comprised of 310 brain glioma segmentation labels and detailed DICOM data, and is available at https://github.com/QIAGENbioinformatics/brats18.  We also provide a containerized version of the tool, available at https://quay.io/registry.  We hope this contribution will facilitate widespread adoption of the tool, thereby bridging the gap between the clinical and the machine learning community.  This paper is accompanied by a tutorial available online.

Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a classical post-hoc model utilizing surrogates faces the problem of explanation coherence, often resulting in inconsistent connections between the model's behavior and the provided information. To address these issues, this paper presents an innovative LIME-RS model, which leverages positive and negative regularization terms to maintain explanation stability and accuracy. The experiments conducted on real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness of the new approach, outperforming existing solutions in terms of both evaluation metrics and user preferences. The primary implications of this research are that future models should prioritize explanation constancy in addition to accuracy, and developers should conduct human-centric evaluation studies to validate their model's performance. We obtain our results by deviating from the conventional learning theory paradigm, which typically prioritizes adversarial robustness. We introduce an effect where the medium is warped by the particle's motion, creating additional friction. This new frictional effect depends on the particle's velocity and acceleration. We compare this with the traditional frictional effect, which depends solely on velocity. Both types of friction are coupled. We demonstrate that when accounting for both forms of friction, the particle's motion is dampened in a manner that approximates exponential decay. We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems. Furthermore, we illustrate that in the Lagrangian context, we achieve optimal results with metric-dependent bounds, while in the Eulerian context, we establish a universal bound for Lipschitz constants across all relevant metrics. As a consequence, we demonstrate that solutions for the Hunter-Saxton equation, both in its Eulerian and Lagrangian forms, exhibit Lipschitz stability for the entire time interval $[0,+\infty)$. We also investigate how this stability evolves over time for the Hunter-Saxton equation, and we show that in the Eulerian framework, the initial conditions play a crucial role in determining the Lipschitz constant for the solution. Building upon this understanding, we extend our analysis to include $\alpha$-dissipative solutions for the extended Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on both its Eulerian and Lagrangian formulations. We then delve into the investigation of temporal Lipschitz stability for the Camassa-Holm vortex patch system, both in its Eulerian and Lagrangian frameworks, before concluding our study by examining the temporal Lipschitz stability for weakly compressible Euler equations in its Lagrangian framework. We note that in the cases of the Hunter-Saxton equation and weakly compressible Euler equations, the analysis is restricted to the Eulerian framework, given that these equations cannot be expressed in a Lagrangian form that is dependent solely on the solution variable. We illustrate that in these situations, the choice of metrics depends on the solution itself, rendering the solution-dependent metrics non-adaptive and ineffective for use in the solution-dependent context. However, we demonstrate that in the solution-independent context, the solution-dependent metrics do achieve optimal results with metric-dependent bounds. We conclude our study with several open questions and potential avenues for further exploration in the realm of temporal Lipschitz stability for partial differential equations.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features as sequential processes. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech. Additionally, a listener survey measuring the naturalness of synthesised speech using median-based generation showed comparable results to HMM-GMM approaches, while revealing a preference for the distribution of durations to be closer to the actual histogram of the training data. Median-based generation is found to yield higher quality results than other methods in this investigation. Further applications of this method, beyond speech synthesis, are discussed, drawing on concepts from categorical modelling in the fields of economics and biology. We also explore how it can be extended to estimate the means of durations, enabling a hybrid strategy that balances representativeness and synthesis. A thorough comparison with existing state-of-the-art HMM-GMM method in terms of modelling any duration distribution is conducted, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Moreover, the possibility of embedding a duration model within a transformer architecture is also considered. This research is part of a larger effort to develop a unified framework for modelling speech and acoustic features as sequential processes. A novel control strategy for an industrial robot is presented, which utilizes additional sensors to counteract dynamic vibrations and improve position tracking accuracy. The proposed flatness-based control approach enables seamless tracking of desired trajectories on industrial robots with or without supplementary sensors, by compensating for predictive errors detected by the additional encoders. Experimental results on a KUKA IR325 demonstrate that the addition of flatness-based control, in conjunction with encoders only, achieves a 50% improvement in maximum acceleration compared to standard position control. Furthermore, when combined with flatness-based control and encoders and torque sensors, a 90% reduction in dynamic position deviation is observed, allowing for increased overspeeding by a factor of three compared to standard position control with encoders. Overall, the flatness-based control strategy demonstrates its robustness and versatility as a suitable solution for a wide range of industrial robotics applications. One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at each atomic site, effectively dividing the integrand. Although the unaltered Becke scheme exhibits slow convergence when applied to free electronic states, we discovered that our modified scheme remains accurate in such situations. We compared our method to traditional approaches that use uniform grids with a limited number of points - 96, 256, and 4096 - in calculations of Mie theory molecules, a model for bulk and surface dielectric properties. Our results show that our scheme achieves precise results with 96 points, similar to the more detailed 4096-point grid in perfect accuracy. In contrast, a 256-point grid yields intermediate results. Compared to other methods for calculating integrals in complex systems, our scheme achieves precise results with fewer grid points than some of the literature methods. For example, a 256-point grid in our scheme is equivalent to approximately two Hartree points, calculated by Ligabue et al. using a 4096-point grid in their scheme. We also compared our method to traditional approaches that use adaptative grids with a limited number of points - 64 and 2048 - in calculations of a homogenous electron gas. Our results show that our scheme achieves precise results with 64 points, similar to the more detailed 2048-point grid in perfect accuracy. In contrast, a 256-point grid yielded intermediate results. We hope that our method will be a valuable tool for calculating electronic integrals in complex systems. We plan to further improve our method to speed up the calculation of these integrals in our next work.

As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV by positioning it on top of boron nitride or in between boron nitride layers. The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery due to its approximate age of around 10,000 years. Since its age doesn't match typical core-collapse supernova ages, we've conducted 3D stellar dynamic simulations to simulate the trajectories of supernovae within the galaxy's radial density peak, where Sgr A East resides. These simulations consider various models of stellar dispersal and a central black hole's influence. They show that a supernova leading to Sgr A East would have had to explode about 20 parsecs from the present-day remnant's location. This distance is consistent with two possible age scenarios for Sgr A East: either it's older than what's generally believed due to a more distant explosion, or the black hole has interacted with the exploding star close to its current position. After the explosion, the stellar material would have taken around 10,000 years to reach its current location within the galaxy. Furthermore, our simulations suggest that Sgr A East likely formed from a region with a very high stellar density, around 100 times that of the average, due to a more distant explosion location. This high density explains why Sgr A East's location doesn't match typical supernova predictions. Sgr A East's age could be around 10,000 years if it formed from a neutron star, or it could be older if the neutron star transformed into a black hole after a long time. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. Interestingly, our data suggest that even within underprivileged groups, younger and non-white individuals were more likely to be exposed to COVID coverage. These findings are significant because they indicate a disparity in information access contributing to existing health and political disparities. Furthermore, our study offers essential insights for local news outlets on how to effectively reach and inform their audiences, particularly during a pandemic. Ultimately, our work has implications for local news COVID coverage efficiency and equity during public health crises. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless in three-dimensional applications with the assistance of a fast multipole method. However, there are unforeseen fluctuations in energy and angular momentum quantities when utilizing this method, particularly evident in particle-in-cell plasmas simulations. These inaccuracies have been identified as stemming from a mistake in the computation of divergence used in the method, coupled with a particular form of Newton's second law. Specifically, these errors result in a gradual deterioration of conserved angular momentum. We present a revised version of the fast multipole method that rectifies this issue and ensure the precise conservation of angular momentum. We also make available the source code for this purpose. Through diverse numerical tests, we verify that this modified algorithm maintains the conservation of angular momentum in SPH simulations across different domains, including static conditions, rigid body rotations, and planetary motion. These numerical tests further reveal that this modification causes minimal impact on existing simulations and results in negligible differences for most applications, yet it is crucial for scenarios where angular momentum conservation is vital, such as dynamics of rigid bodies and planetary systems. We also explore the performance difference between using and not using this modification in planetary system simulations to understand the practical implications. We believe this advancement to have significant influence on SPH-based fluid dynamics and physics research. We have also embedded a new conservative version of the N-body algorithm into PETSc, a widely-used scientific computing framework, and made the code available at https://github.com/petsc-ts Tec petsc-ts. We examine how students with varying abilities can learn from more experienced teachers in a shared educational setting. Unlike conventional models which assume each student receives a full training course from each teacher, we develop a novel model where students are assigned a portion of the curriculum by each teacher, based on their specific needs. Our model utilizes data augmentation to simulate the partial curriculum assigned to each student by each teacher, allowing for more efficient learning. We implement this concept in both non-adversarial and adversarial settings, and demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve improved results on selected benchmark datasets. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a foundation for further investigation into curriculum-based learning methodologies. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/tony269/PCML.git. For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues. This method also enables direct calculation and estimation bounds for the area of the Siegel disk, which can be utilized to infer the automorphism's transcendence. Consequently, K3 surface Picard numbers can be determined transcendence-free. This study culminates in a list of K3 surface codes with designated properties based on computationally derived data. The research further sketches an approach to proving that K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks are almost always algebraic. Additionally, a novel observation is made about the relationship between K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks and their Lefschetz-type formulas. Finally, coding theory implications and applications arise from these findings. The related code family $\mathcal{C}_{h,g}$, derived from K3 surface symplectic data, is particularly noteworthy as it exhibits a Lefschetz-type structure. The research demonstrates that for any given even $h\geq22$, the existence of $\mathcal{C}_{h,g}$ for some $g$ is equivalent to the existence of a K3 surface code $\mathcal{C}_{18,g'}$ for some $g'$ such that $\sigma(\mathcal{C}_{h,g})>\sigma(\mathcal{C}_{18,g'})$. This result highlights an intriguing connection between these two code families. The study also introduces several open questions to guide future research. The main contribution of this paper is to develop a computational algorithm that can efficiently approximate the genus of a dense graph, using a polynomial-time memory space. Given an arbitrary precision parameter epsilon greater than zero, this algorithm can calculate a graph's genus value with an accuracy of epsilon, requiring a time complexity of O(n^(2 + epsilon)) and a memory complexity of O(n), where n represents the graph's number of vertices. Additionally, this algorithm can identify whether a graph's genus value falls within a specific integer range by utilizing a sub-quadratic time complexity of O(n^(1.9859]). Notably, this algorithm's performance surpasses previous best results in this area, and it can also be adapted to approximate other graph layout parameters, such as the Euler genus, surface arboricity, and Euler genus arboricity. A detailed explanation of the algorithm's methodology and implementation will also be provided and reviewed in the final section of this research. Furthermore, an analogous algorithm can be developed for approximating the embedding number of a graph, defined as the least common multiple of its genus values for all possible orientations, utilizing a time complexity of O(n log n + n log (log t)^(1/d) with a time exponent of 0.158. Finally, this research also reveals that identifying the exact genus value of a graph is, in fact, an NP-complete problem when considering the genus value itself as the problem in question. However, interestingly, this problem becomes partially NP-complete when limited to only considering non-negative genus values. A comprehensive list of open problems and research questions is also presented in the final section of this research. A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. Despite the advantages of machine-learning based models, they are not yet capable of replacing expert judgment due to limitations in handling complex behavior interactions and contextual dependencies. The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference marginal exist. This paper explores what happens when the Schrödingers problem has no solution, a scenario that has received little attention in previous research. Our results demonstrate that, even without a solution, the Sinkhorn algorithm still converges, although the possibility of diverging remains if the reference marginal is also non-existent. This paper also examines how the algorithm's performance is impacted by the absence of a solution in practice, using a real-world applied problem as a test case. Our empirical findings suggest that, in most cases, the algorithm still produces a satisfactory solution even when no theoretical one exists. This highlights the importance- and often necessity- of formulating a regularization technique to ensure algorithmic success. As such, this paper also introduces a novel regularization method and demonstrates its effectiveness through our empirical evaluation. Further examples and abstractions of this method can be found in a supplementary document. The presented findings are verifiable through a accompanying Julia notebook available at https://github.com/pszilvas. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, our study focuses on how the diversity of encounters among residents varied over the course of the pandemic using Chicago's taxi cab data from January 2020 to July 2021. By examining the spatial and temporal dimensions of diversity, our research reveals two key findings. Firstly, despite initial decreases in mobility, resident interactions outside their neighborhoods significantly increased in the second pandemic wave, indicating a shift away from pre-pandemic social distancing behaviors. Secondly, our analysis shows that diversity of encounters outside urban areas continued to decline, suggesting that remaining challenges could be addressed through enhanced community engagement and social cohesion initiatives. By quantifying diversity through statistical measurement, our research provides actionable insights for urban planners and policymakers to develop targeted strategies for rebuilding urban spaces that are inclusive, equitable, and resilient. Our findings have significant implications for post-pandemic urban recovery and redevelopment efforts, and can inform a wide range of social science research in urban settings. The conformal field theory description of this limit involves a specific deformation of the Liouville CFT with phi to the power of beta, and we have determined that beta equals two minus the exponent of the string coupling in the semi-classical limit. The action we have derived exactly matches the calculable portion of the action developed by Sachdev and Witten. We have further demonstrated that using path integrals on the worldsheet, with the action we have derived as the Lagrangian, yields the correct tree-level action for JT gravity. We have established that the path integrals on this worldsheet remain Gaussian. We have computed the partition function for this system and verified its equivalence with the Witten diagram partition function for JT gravity. We have analyzed the spectral density, with beta equal to two, and found that it agrees with the semi-classical limit spectral density developed by Stanford and Yang when the latter is generalized by replacing z with phi. In particular, we have found that the location of the branch cut in the spectral density begins at a non-zero value of the imaginary part. We have determined this value as proportional to the exponential of minus the square root of the Lyapunov exponent divided by ten. By setting the Lyapunov exponent equal to zero, we have found that the edge of the branch cut located at a value proportional to the exponential of minus the exponent of the string coupling in the semi-classical limit, with the exponent of beta equal to two, is consistent with the findings of Stanford and Yang. We have analyzed the diffusion constant in the Liouville CFT with phi to the power of beta, with beta equal to two, and found that it is proportional to the exponential of minus the exponent of the string coupling in the semi-classical limit. We have further determined that the string theory is equivalent to a specific pure state quantum mechanics with Hamiltonian derived from the action we have previously determined. We have found that the soliton limit of this quantum mechanics is equivalent to JT gravity. A spacetime with negative energy density can be created by a warp drive propulsion system that allows for space travel at subluminal speeds, overcoming the speed of light limit. This paper presents two new exact solutions for warp drive spacetimes incorporating a perfect fluid and a cosmological constant, in a two-component gravitational field, using a nonlinear algebraic equation. We analyze the energy conditions and causal properties for both solutions and discuss their physical implications. We also compare these solutions with existing warp drive literature. In addition, we identify a new exact solution for Brans-Dicke gravity, which is a scalar-tensor theory of gravity, when the scalar field is set to a constant. We also calculate the energy conditions and causal effects in this case. Both solutions are made available through a public repository for ease of access. Finally, we discuss the theoretical and practical implications of these new exact solutions. This work was supported by the following grants: CSF: 4552 and FS: 3627. TERS is an innovative technique within near-field spectroscopy that offers unparalleled spatial resolution down to the single molecular level. It has the unique capability to gather electromagnetic, chemical, and mechanical data, making it an attractive choice for in-depth analysis of interactions between molecules and surfaces. Theoretical models suggest that the distinct interaction patterns of chemical and electromagnetic effects play a crucial role in TERS's high spatial resolution. Nevertheless, a comprehensive study to independently evaluate these effects in TERS is currently missing. Our work aims to advance in this direction by incorporating both electromagnetic and chemical interactions into a full quantum simulation of TERS. We utilize this model to investigate the interaction between a gold tip and a phenyl ring, taking into account varying tip-molecule distances and orientations. By doing so, we are able to distinguish between the chemical and electromagnetic contributions to TERS images and explore their dependence on parameters such as a short-range chemical interaction and a long-range electromagnetic interaction. Our results confirm that both effects are essential for achieving high spatial resolution in TERS, and demonstrate that the distinct interaction patterns of these effects can provide valuable clues for interpreting TERS images and identifying the spatial origin of resonant signals. By applying our model to a real-world TERS study of melamine, we are able to offer a more plausible chemical explanation for observed resonant signals based on electromagnetic and chemical interactions. Our findings from these numerical experiments align well with available experimental data, highlighting the significant influence of both electromagnetic and chemical effects on single-molecule recognition in TERS. By incorporating these interactions, we are able to achieve improved local image contrast and resolve covalent bonds between melamine and trichlorosilane. Our model suggests that the chemical effect should be the primary consideration for TERS image analysis at short range, whereas both electromagnetic and chemical effects contribute to TERS signals at longer ranges. These interactions can be leveraged to improve accuracy in molecular structure determination and spectroscopy. Our approach may also provide new opportunities for computational design and optimization of TERS experiments. By combining both electromagnetic and chemical interactions into a full quantum simulation of TERS, we are able to achieve higher precision in TERS image analysis and offer novel insights into the underlying mechanisms of this technique. We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to observe 27 nearby galaxies using the K-band, a frequency range where anomalous microwave emission from spinning dust particles is typically detected. The goal was to explore the potential presence of AME in nearby galaxies for the first time. After applying foreground removal methods and subtracting a baseline, we were left with a small number of sources with featureless spectra. Although we didn't observe any unambiguous AME signal in galaxies, we did observe an excess in one source which could be explained by an AME component with a temperature of around 85 K. However, since only a small percentage of the galaxy's area was observed, it is unclear whether this detection corresponds to a galactic or extragalactic origin. Further observations with flat spectra and increased signal-to-noise ratio are needed to confirm the presence of AME in galaxies. The presented data show that ground-based interferometric telescopes can be effective in detecting emission from multiple galaxies simultaneously, increasing the chances of discovering global AME signals. This technique can be applied to other frequencies and observatories, such as the Very Large Radio Telescope, to detect AME in a large collection of galaxies. Additionally, this methodology may serve as a starting point for investigating the emission mechanisms of radio and X-ray non-thermal emissions. Finally, with forthcoming interferometric facilities, such as the Square Kilometer Array, it will be feasible to explore the emission mechanisms behind non-thermal processes in an enormous number of extragalactic sources. By doing so, it will be possible to test cosmological average values for key physical parameters, such as the HI column density and the cosmic density of spinning dust particles. The present study is a preliminary step in this direction, focusing on the microwave regime. For decades, researchers have disputed the cause of the substantial entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using comprehensive density functional theory calculations that also clarified the microscopic origins of the material's dynamism. It appears that the substantial entropy is primarily attributed to the disruption of a hydrogen-bond network framework involving both ammonium and sulfate groups, with multiple degenerate states contributing to the entropy in the high-symmetry phase due to hydrogen atom hopping and ammonium group rotation in and between equivalent positions. Furthermore, this finding points to a promising application of ab initio calculations in identifying other materials exhibiting substantial entropy. Also, we determined that the quantum states driving the Witten index to 1 are Mersenne prime-based states, which are already known to be entangled. We propose that these states, when used in computations involving products of matrices, exhibit contextuality due to their fundamental nature as entangled. This fundamental nature is similar to that of the GHZ state, which is known to be both entangled and maximally contextual. Conversely, we found that states derived from products of matrices do not necessarily exhibit entanglement. When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on shared control focuses on this inference by considering a variety of signal inputs, such as the position of the joystick and vision images. While these approaches are valuable for determining the robot's desired motion, they do not address the issue of whether the human is requesting a specific action, such as picking up an object. We propose that by incorporating conventions into shared control systems, the robot can more effectively identify the task the human is attempting to perform. Conventions enable the robot to distinguish between motions with and without purpose, and can specify which regions of its workspace correspond to high-level actions. While conventional shared control still necessitates human input to define the physical boundaries of tasks, it facilitates more natural and engaging interactions between humans and robots. Conventions can also be communicated through visual indicators, such as a virtual 'joystick' on a display that represents the intended action. By combining a shared control system with convention-based communication, the robot's ability to automatically perform tasks in accordance with human intentions is significantly improved. During a series of user studies, we discovered that our proposed system allowed participants to accomplish more tasks with fewer attempts and with greater efficiency than in cases without conventions. The results of our research indicate that incorporating robot conventions into shared control systems enhances human-robot collaboration and brings the robot's behavior closer to that of a skilled cooperator. The approach is versatile and can be applied to a variety of robotic systems that operate in a variety of environments, as illustrated by its successful deployment in a mobile robot that navigates through a dynamic environment. Furthermore, we have found that incorporating conventions into shared control systems is accessible and intuitive for human operators, as evidenced by user feedback and system designs that we have presented at a number of conferences. The key ideas from our paper have been incorporated into a publicly available, open-source Python library called pyCon - a Python module for cooperative robot systems - which is designed to assist developers in creating conventional shared control systems. The library provides a range of useful features, including a conventional estimator, a variety of action generators, and a module for communicating conventions through visual indicators. The approach is available under a permissive open-source license, allowing researchers and engineers to readily adopt and contribute to it. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, these systems struggle in environments with consistent visual features, causing navigation issues for robots. To overcome this challenge, we've introduced HiTMap, a novel mapping strategy that leverages triangles from a 2D map to build hierarchical, robust data structures. By focusing solely on triangle data, HiTMap avoids feature-based issues and efficiently navigates unfamiliar environments successfully. Computed Tomography (CT) is a crucial imaging technique used in medical, industrial, and many other settings. It employs X-rays of various energy levels to capture images of internal compositions with unique attenuation properties. Since X-ray beams typically consist of multiple energy levels, rather than a single energy, an enhanced image reconstruction model that accounts for polyenergetic beams would be beneficial. Furthermore, we also provided an efficient algorithm to solve this challenging problem. The results show that the proposed model performs well even with data of limited quality and polyenergetic X-ray beams. This model is particularly valuable for devices with sensor degradation problems, as it can improve image reconstruction without altering the X-ray beam settings. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena, but excludes spillover in the direction perpendicular to the metal surfaces, accurately predicts a resonance in the case of a very narrow gap, and this resonance frequency converges to the true resonance frequency as the gap widens. These simulations also reveal the role that electron spillover and nonlocality play in the propagation of light through a narrow gap. Interestingly, we find that electronic surface charges generated by gap-plasmons have partial transverse components due to spillover effects. These transverse components cause anisotropic light propagation through a narrow gap, with different polarization directions for reflection and transmission. However, this anisotropic propagation disappears as the gap widens. In contrast, we find that electronic surface charges parallel to the metal surfaces remain charge-conserving, local, and classical. Furthermore, we show that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena, but excludes parallel spillover, accurately predicts reflection and transmission spectra for various gap geometries, and these spectra converge to the true spectra as the gap widens. These converged spectra match both density functional theory and quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena, but excludes spillover in the limit of vanishing gaps. Lastly, we show that quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena, but excludes parallel spillover, correctly predicts that light propagation through a ring-shaped nanostructure produces a dark area due to spillover effects. These findings highlight the significance of incorporating both electron spillover and nonlocality in quantum hydrodynamics model for nanostructure applications. This research introduces an innovative neural network filter designed to improve
canonical distribution estimates derived from the DTDD algorithm, specifically
to minimize bias in dynamic state estimates. Bias in the estimated dynamic state
can be severe due to BMS (best match only) sampling bias when matching a point cloud to a distribution, which has significant implications for multi-object tracking. A neural network filter is proposed to correct DTDD pose estimates by aligning the BMS sample with the true distribution mean, and it does this by learning to identify the mean of the distribution in 3D point clouds. The learned capability is then applied to correct the DTDD algorithm, and it outperforms existing methods in reducing dynamic state bias. Moreover, the study presents a straightforward method for training the neural network that utilizes synthetic data generation without the need for ground truth labels. The study's findings are grounded in a novel dataset called SynthCity, which allows for the transfer of synthetic data from various angles, regardless of the actual scene geometry. The dataset facilitates the training of the neural network, and it is used to assess the performance of the DTDD algorithm with and without the neural network filter, and it is available at a public repository. Specifically, the study demonstrates that the neural network filter substantially reduces dynamic state bias in DTDD canonical distribution estimates by as much as 47 percent and improves the precision of the estimated object pose by as much as 2.5 meters in the most challenging scenarios. The results also indicate that the neural network filter is robust to changes in the scene, and it outperforms existing methods in tracking performance, with improvements of up to 47 percent when used in conjunction with the simplest of tracking models. On one hand, researchers from dynamical systems are drawn to machine learning for its potential to automatically uncover patterns in data. On the other hand, researchers from machine learning are particularly interested in applying their skills to real-world problems from the physical and biological sciences that have historically been challenging to solve. Applying machine learning to these problems, however, poses significant challenges related to formulating tasks, selecting relevant data, and evaluating outcomes. Additionally, there is a concern that over-reliance on automated methods may compromise the theoretical and computational advancements traditionally pursued in dynamical systems. We discuss some strategies for integrating machine learning into applications from the physical and biological sciences, such as reducing model error and utilizing data from time series analysis to uncover patterns in complex systems. We use reduction techniques from dynamical systems to illustrate how to formulate learning tasks that can be evaluated with neural networks and other machine learning methods. We also provide theoretical and practical approaches for determining the accuracy of these models and leveraging them to make predictions and develop control strategies for complex systems that include chaos. We demonstrate the application of these methods to predicting long-term behavior in systems with chaos, modeling population dynamics, and controlling neural activity. We conclude with some general strategies for successfully incorporating machine learning into collaborations from the physical and biological sciences. We also provide some advice for initiating and continuing cross-disciplinary collaborations that combine machine learning and dynamical systems. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is needed to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars. 

Furthermore, it's discovered that massive cores, regardless of whether they're associated with outflows or not, tend to have higher densities than their less massive counterparts. This implies that in these infrared dark clouds, cores are primarily observed in their diffuse outer regions due to the influence of dust absorption. As a result, the actual densities of these cores are higher than their observed values, especially for massive cores which could explain why they're less frequently detected. 

Lastly, it's worth noting that through the analysis of core properties across the Dragon infrared dark cloud, the relationship between core morphology and intensity of star formation becomes more apparent, with effects of resolution also considered and mitigated. 

In summary, this research significantly advances the understanding of the origin and characteristics of massive star formation, with potential applications to the broader star-forming environment.

In neural machine translation, the attention model currently used is based on a specific point in time, mapping destinations to sources via learned weights. However, this single-perspective approach can result in an inconsistent alignment between past and future predictions during decoding. This leads to a significant issue where previously generated elements may be invalid due to changes in alignment, causing challenging NMT systems to fail completely. In our study, we address this alignment discrepancy by introducing a novel look-ahead attention mechanism that takes into account multiple past historical elements and predicts future alignment by considering multiple future predictions. This innovative design captures the global alignment more accurately and results in substantial improvements for challenging NMT tasks, especially when combined with other methods. Experiments on the WMT19 exact translation tasks show that our system surpasses the current state-of-the-art performance. This difficulty stems partly from limitations in available observational data and the need to reconcile various theoretical models, which often require different levels of fine-tuning. The aim of this review is to provide an in-depth examination of the interstellar media of dwarf galaxies, with a primary focus on those that have visible stars. The ISMs of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, including luminous and dark galaxies, are also explored through the lens of existing observations and with the consideration of forthcoming advances in the field. However, integrating speaker-awareness into existing models is common practice, which doesn't fully address the complexity of this task. To tackle this issue, a novel transformer-based model is introduced, called TS2-Net, which token-shifts and token-selects for enhanced performance. This model is built upon a dual-stream architecture that combines visual and linguistic features, and it employs a multi-head attention mechanism with a constraint to prioritize more informative visual tokens. As a result, it surpasses current state-of-the-art models when tested on various benchmarks, including MSRVTT, MSVD, MSCOCompetition, and VATEX. Furthermore, TS2-Net demonstrates superior performance compared to existing models when tested on challenging scenarios, including when the number of training video frames is reduced. To promote further research, the model's code and data will be made available. All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, sometimes with catastrophic results. 
This raises critical safety concerns that must be addressed by researchers, who are also exploring new ethical challenges as AI computing grows in importance. 
In an effort to mitigate these concerns, engineers are now involved in AI development, applying their expertise to ensure systems function as intended. 
This shift has led to a movement of augmenting AI with human-like intentions, referred to as Augmented Artificial Intelligence. 
This paper aims to introduce the concept of augmented AI, discussing both existing AI and the emerging technology, and outlining a comprehensive framework with accompanying examples. 
The authors propose that augmented AI can be viewed as a complex system consisting of four interconnected layers: fundamental principles, algorithms, models, and operational processes. 
By adopting a multi-faceted approach, researchers and practitioners can work together to integrate human values into AI systems, ensuring they function as intended in real-world situations. 
Additionally, the paper highlights both practical and theoretical benefits of augmented AI, providing a foundational understanding of this emerging technology. 
Ultimately, the paper sets the stage for further discussions on the subject and may inspire readers to explore augmented AI as a means of advancing and ensuring responsible AI behaviors. 
A companion demonstration is available at https://augmentedai.github.io/ and the code can be accessed at https://github.com/AAI-LUM on GitHub.

By introducing a spin-orbit coupling factor γ, we observe the emergence of finite-wavevector condensation of bosons. The superfluid properties of these bosons can manifest as homogeneous, phase-twisted, or orbital ordering patterns. Through our analysis, we investigate the phase twist and identify three types of twist states: non-topological, fractional, and topological. In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a pivotal step. Gaussian Processes rely on a kernel function that defines similarity between data points, and specifying one involves significant expertise in the underlying problem. We present Gaintel, a novel system that dynamically selects and optimizes Gaussian Process kernels using elementary mathematical expressions, eliminating the need for domain-specific expertise. We utilize Genetic Algorithms to evolve kernels in large-scale graph classification tasks and graph representation learning tasks, and Gaintel outperforms state-of-the-art methods in graph classification while requiring significantly less domain-specific knowledge. Gaintel's source code is publicly available.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have shown that deep learning models can effectively clean noisy signals and extract meaningful data. By combining a deep denoising autoencoder with a Gaussian-like model, we can achieve even better results, but this method may not be accurate in cases of extreme noise levels. Therefore, we have developed an innovative CNN-RNN model, which we call the Tirami-su, to efficiently clean noisy signals and accurately extract IBIs from ECG data, even in the most challenging environments. Our new model represents a substantial improvement over its predecessors and has demonstrated exceptional performance on challenging datasets. With its advanced capabilities, we have set a new standard in ECG-based IBI estimation and achieved error rates of 1.48/100b, 2.18/100b, and 3.87/100b on MUSE, NFBC2, and public challenge datasets, respectively. Notably, we have surpassed all existing state-of-the-art models in terms of overall performance and have achieved superior results on all three mentioned datasets. Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs, which involves mapping vertices and edges to points in a low-dimensional space while preserving node relationships. However, real-world networks frequently undergo changes with new additions, deletions, or updates to existing connections. This dynamic nature presents both opportunities and challenges for network analysis, as it enables the examination of temporal trends but demands efficient handling of growth and relationships to reduce complexity. To address embedding dynamic graphs, which require low-dimensional representations while capturing temporal information, various methods have been developed. This work presents a comprehensive review of dynamic graph embedding, discussing the different types of temporal dynamics, experimental settings, and theoretical foundations. We also compare existing static and dynamic graph embedding techniques, emphasizing common approaches, variations, and outlining a framework for dynamic graph embedding that distills key aspects. This survey aims to provide valuable insights for researchers and developers working on dynamic graph embedding. Moreover, we discuss its potential applications and data sets suitable for evaluation, highlighting various directions for future research. Finally, this survey is expected to aid both researchers and practitioners in understanding dynamic graph embedding. With the emergence of new methods, it's anticipated that dynamic graph embedding will continue to evolve. Deep Metric Learning has emerged as a prominent strategy for metric learning, focusing on forming meaningful similarity structures between data points. A crucial step in Deep Metric Learning involves parameterising a metric as a similarity measure between two random variables. Researchers have previously used Gaussian metrics, specifically Gaussian distribution's mean scale combination, to achieve this. However, a recent study demonstrates that using a radial distribution with divergent measures such as Hellinger and total variation divergences leads to more effective data embeddings. Building on these findings, our study introduces a novel radial distribution-based metric that utilizes the minimum flow problem's distance measures, known as Sinkhorn distances. We test the introduced metric on widely-used datasets, including CUB-200-2011 and CAPE. The results reveal that the newly-proposed metric outperforms existing approaches, highlighting its potential for Deep Metric Learning. Furthermore, we provide a mathematical justification for the convergence of the proposed metric to its optimal form as the minimum flow problem's scaling factor approaches infinity. The introduced approach's success can be attributed to its well-defined and smooth nature, differing from previous divergent measures. Consequently, this method is suitable for use in Deep Metric Learning and can be employed to develop novel and effective metric learning algorithms. We introduce an novel approach that enhances semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. We separate the speech representations into acoustic and linguistic elements using inter-domain loss techniques. We utilize CycleGAN to apply a linguistic loss that mimics a speaker-independent model, decoupling speaker identity from the representations, and integrates a sentence-level alignment loss that associates input speech with target text. Experimentation on Si-284 and Voxforge datasets reveals improved performance after applying our method, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. Notably, it surpasses domain-adaptive fine-tuning methods in efficiency. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach effectively extracts speaker-independent representations that surpass baseline models in speaker verification tasks. We release our code and dataset annotations to facilitate reproducibility.

This thesis delves into the application of active inference, a Bayesian framework, to facilitate independent robot navigation. The key idea is that agents seek to maximize their expected entropy gains by selecting actions that lead to the most informative environments. However, as illustrated through case studies, unmodified active inference can result in unrealistic navigation strategies due to an overemphasis on environmental uncertainty at the expense of other considerations. To address these limitations, this research introduces a novel within-a-active-inference approach, building upon the concept of inside-a-active-inference suggested by Chantemayen-Skull (2020). The within-a-active-inference method involves embedding multiple active inference models, each representing different levels of environmental uncertainty, and using a higher-level model to determine when to switch to a more or less uncertain model. The approach was evaluated in both simulated and real-world conditions on two complex robot navigation tasks: mapping an unfamiliar environment and through narrow windows. The within-a-active-inference method demonstrated notable improvements in task completion while also reducing computational costs by leveraging previously derived models. The successful implementation of within-a-active-inference marks a crucial step in the development of multi-faceted, layered strategies for active inference agents and has significant implications for machine learning and autonomous systems that operate in dynamic and uncertain environments. The presented research represents a contribution to the ongoing efforts of the probabilistic robotics and autonomous systems communities. The associated code and videos can be found on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/tonyoski/deepactiveinferencenavigation. However, this report deviates from the original research by integrating deep active inference and exploring the application of within-a-active-inference to the navigation of robots that need to complete tasks in environments that are difficult to access through narrow openings. The purpose of this study is to demonstrate that several prominent text classification models can be viewed as manifestations of a family of functions, which we term "Sibyl" variants. To achieve this, we establish a unified framework using transformers and introduce a novel parameterization for robust function transformations. This transformation framework enables the creation of a robust model capable of withstanding various types of input manipulations without compromising performance, as illustrated by our experimental results across four text classification datasets in various settings. Furthermore, our unifying approach enables the identification of common underlying structures among the various models and allows us to compare their functional relationships. This not only sheds light on their mathematical connections but also holds significant practical implications for developing model-agnostic interventions, as exemplified by our numerical results. Moreover, our framework provides insights for developing novel, adaptive interventions that can respond to changing data conditions, as demonstrated by our results on a dynamic variant of the STL-1 dataset that dynamically shifts from positive to negative class labels at fixed time points. This model is particularly noteworthy as it operates without relying on pre-trained language models, requiring only task-specific training. Finally, our experimental results on English and non-English datasets not only verify the robustness of our models under different types of input perturbations (insertion, deletion, substitution) but also reveal their potential vulnerabilities under specific attacks, as illustrated by our results on the Amazon Polite Language Dataset. This study not only contributes to a deeper mathematical understanding of the underlying functions but also provides insights for developing model-agnostic interventions capable of withstanding various types of input manipulations. Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish the theoretical validity of these approaches. In this research, we develop a framework for proactive learning of linear representations through a common, shared matrix. We prove that this method is capable of achieving optimal performance on multiple tasks and that a suitable objective exists, which can be optimized through stochastic gradient descent. Furthermore, we show that our approach yields representations with orthogonal columns, mirroring findings in over-parameterized training, where an optimal linear model exists and can be located through generic optimization methods. We also introduce a task similarity objective that enhances representation learning between tasks and provide theoretical validation of this method by demonstrating its ability to achieve optimal, low-error representations through theoretical risk bounds. By developing a meta-learning framework with theoretical backing, we are able to provide the first theoretical insights into meta-learning techniques. In our experiments, we observe that our approach generalizes well across multiple tasks and we identify a suitable objective that enables the transfer of knowledge across tasks. Our results suggest that a linear approach to representation learning has theoretical merits and may be a reliable starting point for developing meta-learning algorithms. Ultimately, we aim to expand the scope of our framework to accommodate non-linear representations, a goal that we pursue in our subsequent work. 

Our initial contributions are as follows: 

1) We create a novel meta-learning framework with a theoretical connection to representation learning that we prove to be effective in achieving low error rates on multiple tasks.

3) We show that a stochastic gradient descent can be applied to our framework in order to achieve optimal results.

4) We develop a theoretical model for assessing the performance of our approach through theoretical risk bounds and we demonstrate the success of our model through experimental validation. 

5) We apply our model to a variety of experimental settings in order to achieve a deeper understanding of the impact of different parameters on the performance of our model and to identify the most critical factors that contribute to optimal results.
