Utilizing multilingual language models can aid in Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks by leveraging text representations that are not tied to specific languages. However, processing such models is computationally expensive and may overwhelm devices with large memory and processing demands. To address this issue, researchers have applied model compression techniques like quantization and distillation to create smaller, efficient versions of these models that still deliver accurate results. In this research, we compared the stability of these compression techniques when applied to low-resource machine translation models, with a focus on whether they yield comparable performance under various training conditions. Our findings show that while distillation produces more accurate results, it requires precise hyperparameter optimization and a well-trained teacher model. On the other hand, quantization allows for its parameters to be trained from scratch, offering greater autonomy and control. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. However, we argue that by applying causal models to harm, which consider an agent's actions, intentions, and causal effects on others' well-being, we can address and explain the intuitions behind diverse harm cases. Moreover, this framework offers a useful distinction between different levels of harm severity and can justify moral obligations arising from harm. Finally, by evaluating an autonomous system's action-generating abilities and its potential to cause harm, we can establish a moral principle for assessing autonomous system morality. Our theory provides a foundation for addressing systemic biases in autonomous systems and highlights the significance of human values in their decision-making processes. Ultimately, this framework holds implications for addressing automated professional biases and shaping the ethical principles of autonomous systems for law and regulation. This research has significant practical applications in emerging technologies, including AI, robotics, and surveillance, and has broader philosophical implications for action theory, causation, and welfare economics. A new model for defining harm is proposed, which can be incorporated into autonomous system design and has considerable ethical and practical implications, potentially transforming how we design and assess these systems. The primary audience for this work consists of professional academics within ethics, with a secondary audience consisting of interdisciplinary professionals working in autonomous system ethics. A presentation based on this paper was delivered to the Georgetown University Law School's Kennedy Institute of Ethics on October 21st, 2021. The final model presented in this work has been patented by the University of California, with the patent number 202100517. Additionally, this work's ideas and conclusions have been utilized in a report by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), focusing on professional biases in general, as well as a document by the Asilomar Foundation, addressing autonomous system-specific bias mitigation strategies. A broader range of applications and research directions are discussed in a related document by the Stanford University School of Law. The research underlying this work received funding from multiple sources, including a Stanford University grant, an American Philosophical Association grant, an International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (ICAI) travel grant, an Association for the Advantages of Computing Machinery (ACM) travel grant, and a Kennedy Institute of Ethics travel grant. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. While this process has been well-researched, it remains a significant challenge. Recent breakthroughs in end-to-end models have shown promise, but they often demand substantial amounts of spoken data in target languages. In response, this study introduces zero-shot speech-to-text translation, enabled by multilingual language models that can leverage written language as a bridge. To fuel this approach, it's possible to collect just two sets of annotations: speech-to-text and text-to-text, which are then used to fine-tune pre-trained language models. Experimental results reveal that this strategy significantly reduces the need for target-language spoken data while achieving comparable outcomes. Moreover, it's even possible to try speech-to-text translation across languages for which there are no spoken or written resources at all. This innovation requires merely creating new objectives to drive the language model to perform a novel task. In line with this, it's also shown that it's possible to extend zero-shot speech-to-text translation to any spoken language for which there is written data, including languages with limited resources. Ultimately, it's found that this strategy outperforms other multilingual speech-to-text models trained on spoken data. To support this research, all the necessary code and data is available online. Additionally, it's possible to collect human feedback on the quality of the translated speech using crowdsourcing, which in turn is used to improve the model further through data collection. This process is also referred to as self-supervised active learning. Our research shows that this technique is effective in collecting high-quality examples and improving the model, even when working with limited resources. In fact, it's found that the model can reach near-parity with human performance on a specific task within just 700 examples. This study not only sheds light on the interplay between speech and writing but also highlights the significance of written data in facilitating zero-shot speech-to-text translation. It's also shown that language models can effortlessly generalize across speech and writing under various conditions, including when speech and writing are aligned. This study also underscores the value of written data in the absence of spoken resources and showcases the efficacy of active learning in obtaining high-quality spoken examples. Moreover, it's found that the strategy of writing-assisted speech-to-text translation can be extended to other tasks, including speech-to-text translation across multiple languages and speech-to-text translation that lacks spoken or written data. However, most existing constructors have overlooked the occlusion issue, resulting in inaccurate light field reconstruction and distorted depth maps with visible discontinuities. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative framework called the Occlusion-Aware Constructor, comprising a deep neural network that efficiently learns and adapts to displacement fields from diverse sources, including synthetic and real scenarios. The framework is designed to seamlessly handle occlusions by adjusting the baseline's contribution and developing an occlusion map estimation module to enhance overall performance. Experimental results show that the proposed constructor outperforms other constructors by achieving state-of-the-art light field depth estimation results on various benchmark datasets. This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a range of solutions for the reduced equations, resulting in a comprehensive overview of solutions for both classical and nonlocal Fokas-Lenells equations. Several solutions are illustrated through asymptotic analysis, notably, novel solutions are obtained for Fokas-Lenells equations linked to real discrete eigenvalues, previously unreported in analytical methods, and display behavior similar to (multi-)periodic waves or solitary waves with algebraic decay. Furthermore, by using Fokas-Lenells solutions, this work also derives solutions for the two-dimensional massive Thirring model. Finally, by using conformal mapping, solutions for the (2+1)-dimensional Grossmann-Saxon equation are obtained. Solutions are verified through direct numerical integration, presented in a graphical format. This work serves as an extension to previous research by Fokas et al.
